subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. In view of the fact that, according to the figures on unemployment released by the bureau of statistics last night, unemployment both in absolute and relative terms is higher than in the corresponding periods of 1959 and 1958 and, indeed, higher than in any corresponding period since the great depression-

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext: -is the minister now in a position to tell the house how the government intends to deal with this most disturbing national situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in response to some of the statements made by the hon. member for Essex East I wish to say that in the opinion of the government the situation, as we have stated in the past, is always serious as long as there are people unemployed, but it is only half as serious as it was in the years 1935 to 1940 when the hon. member was a member of the government. According to this release there are 250,000 more people working than last month and 140,000 more people working than in the same period last year. The government is always looking at the situation and reviewing it. I am sure the hon. member will find that the government, in its efforts to look after the people of this country, will devise ways and means to rectify the situation, and when that is done an announcement will be made as usual.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. Would the minister care to inform the house what the government feels employment prospects are for the near future, and whether in the opinion of the government there is likely to be a reduction in the number of unemployed in the near future compared with a year ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext:
The hon. member has asked me to foretell the future and I decline to do that,
because I would not want to be quoted at this time, not knowing exactly what the situation may be.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext: It is worse and it is going to get worse under this administration.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. In view of the admittedly serious situation, does the Minister of Labour not think this house ought to be given an opportunity of at least co-operating with an organization being set up in another place to deal with this particular problem? Is it not a disgrace that parliament is denied this opportunity?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would say this. The sooner I see any evidence of co-operation from the hon. member for Essex East, the better it will be for the economy of this country.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext: I wonder if I could put a question to the Prime Minister. Notwithstanding the arrangements that have previously been made, would the Prime Minister consider having the estimates of the Department of Labour called this week so that at least there can be a debate in this house on this most important domestic question?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext: The progress made in calling the various departments depends on the co-operation received from all parts of the house. I am sure that when it is appropriate to have these departments before the house, and when matters already before the house have been cleared away, then an opportunity will be given to the hon. gentleman to discuss these matters.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: FOOD BANK-REPORTED SUGGESTION BY U.S. VICE PRESIDENT
speechtext:
May I
address a question to the Prime Minister. Has the Prime Minister's attention been drawn to, and does he care to comment upon, a recent statement by Vice President Nixon of the United States with respect to the establishment of a United Nations food pool?

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: FOOD BANK-REPORTED SUGGESTION BY U.S. VICE PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a number of occasions in recent years I have advocated the

Inquiries of the Ministry paramount importance of making surplus food stocks available for consumption in parts of the world where food shortages occur or might occur. Indeed, in December, 1957 I advocated the establishment of a NATO food bank which, as yet, has not received the complete support of the various nations in NATO.
When I was in Washington on June 3 I discussed with the President of the United States, not this particular matter but the urgency of working out some satisfactory arrangement for the distribution and utilization of surplus foodstuffs.
The house will also recall that as a result of the food for peace conference held in Washington in May of 1959 there is now in existence an international body known as the wheat utilization committee, the establishment of which was designed to find means of utilizing food surpluses for beneficial purposes. This committee, on which Canada is represented, will have its next semi-annual meeting in Ottawa in this coming July.
The Nixon proposal is one that envisages the co-operation of the countries within the United Nations. Certainly the matter has been discussed on occasions in the past, but there has been no evidence of any support for such a plan from the U.S.S.R. or those countries adhering to the views of the U.S.S.R. However, the suggestion is one that deserves the fullest consideration, for all of us are desirous of assuring that surpluses shall be used to the end that poverty will be met and hunger assuaged in the parts of the world where today food is not available.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FOOD BANK-REPORTED SUGGESTION BY U.S. VICE PRESIDENT
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question. Has there in fact been any serious discussion at the NATO council of the proposal for a NATO food bank, and if so what has been the result of that consideration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: FOOD BANK-REPORTED SUGGESTION BY U.S. VICE PRESIDENT
speechtext: There have been discussions on various occasions regarding a food bank, but there has not been that unanimity that characterizes the opinion of Canadians as a whole.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: WHOOPING CRANES
subsubtopic: RAILWAY ROUTE
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Will he be good enough to comment on the

editorial appearing in last night's Ottawa Journal entitled "A Rare Bird for the Future". For the purpose of putting the record straight will he advise whether it is not correct that the whooping cranes referred to have their present nesting grounds in Wood Buffalo national park along the proposed eastern route of the railway to Great Slave lake, and that these rare birds would not be disturbed by a railroad constructed along the western route; which would not only make the whooping cranes very happy but would have the incidental effect of bringing much joy and relief to some 12,000 people in the Peace river area who have been waiting for over a quarter of a century for this railway?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: WHOOPING CRANES
subsubtopic: RAILWAY ROUTE
speechtext:
I have seen the editorial in question, Mr. Speaker, and I immediately confirm the fact that the statement made about the choice of the route, namely that it should be the eastern route to keep away from the nesting ground of the whooping cranes, is not true. The whooping cranes, about 30 of them in number, nest in Wood Buffalo national park.
I should like to point out also that in a letter to me of June 1 the president of the Audubon society pointed out, his understanding, which is correct, namely that no route so far is in any sense "final or even accurate". I have no doubt that whatever route is recommended by the royal commission or finally chosen for the railway, it will be possible to establish it in such a fashion that ample protection will be given to the breeding ground of these rare birds. I want to assure the hon. member that I fully share his concern that these birds will not be imperilled.

subtopic: WHOOPING CRANES
subsubtopic: RAILWAY ROUTE
speechtext: should like to ask a supplementary question. Will the minister inform the house whether he has received from the United States wildlife authorities any representations in connection with the preservation of these whooping cranes?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speechtext: I shall be obliged to take that supplementary question as notice.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESEARCH ON LIVE VIRUS POLIO VACCINE
speechtext:
I should
like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Is the Department of National Health and Welfare engaged in research on a live virus polio vaccine? Also, is this oral vaccine to be made available in Canada? If so, to what extent?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monieilh (Minisfer of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESEARCH ON LIVE VIRUS POLIO VACCINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer is yes to the first part of the hon. member's question, as trials of this vaccine have been in progress in Canada since February of this year. Members of my department are directly associated with this continuing project, which is receiving federal assistance through national health grants.
No live polio virus vaccine is licensed in Canada at the present time. Following a review of recent information, the national technical advisory committee on live poliomyelitis vaccines on June 20 recommended limited

Inquiries of the Ministry and well supervised field trials of live polio virus vaccines which have received the necessary approval of this department. My department will continue its co-operation in the planning of such trials and study of applications for assistance under the national health grants program. Any decision as to use for the public will depend upon the findings.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RESEARCH ON LIVE VIRUS POLIO VACCINE
speechtext:

supplementary question. I wonder whether the minister could tell the house, if he has the information with him, how many of the considerable number of cases of paralytic polio reported so far this year in Canada are of the people who have previously been vaccinated with the Salk vaccine.

I have read the report in Le Devoir and the officials of the board of broadcast governors are at present conducting hearings in Halifax. (2)	Section 20 of the said act is further amended by adding thereto the following subsections:
"(10) Where property of a corporation that was depreciable property of a prescribed class has, on the making of a receiving order or the filing of an assignment for the benefit of creditors of the corporation, become vested in a trustee in bankruptcy, the property of the corporation of that class shall be deemed, for the purpose of this section and regulations made under paragraph (a) of subsection (1) of section 11, to have been disposed of by the corporation at that time for an amount equal to the undepreciated capital cost thereof to the corporation immediately before that time, and to have been acquired by the trustee at that time at a capital cost equal to that amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will be pleased to deal with this point, and to deal with the kind of criticism in which the hon. member indulged last night in regard to notice. The hon. member has been in this house for 15 years, and I doubt very much whether in all that time he has seen the annual bill to amend the Income Tax Act passed without amendments being introduced in the committee of the whole, because these always arise. The only difference between what is being done now and last year and what was

done before is that previously, under my predecessors, there was no advance notice given of the proposed amendments. Now, in order to give the house as much notice as possible, I have been following the practice of giving notice of the amendments. I did that with respect to the amendments to the budget resolutions, and they appeared in Votes and Proceedings for May 6.
These three amendments to the present bill, Mr. Chairman, I gave to the house last Friday afternoon as soon as they were available. This bill was introduced on June 6. It was to have been proceeded with on June 13. The hon. member did not want to proceed then and asked that it be put over. We did not proceed with it. It was only called again on June 20. These amendments relate to matters that have come to our attention in that period, and notice has been given to the house as soon as it was possible to do so. As a matter of fact I came into the chamber late last Friday afternoon and asked the house to give leave to revert to motions so these amendments could be made a matter of record on Friday. At the same time I gave copies of the amendments to both parties in opposition so they would have an opportunity of reviewing them over the week end.
If the hon. member has not chosen to do his work on these amendments over the week end, all I can say is that I think the practice is one of which the house approves. The alternative, I suppose, is to revert to the practice that existed during the time the hon. member was a parliamentary assistant, and not to give any notice to the house at all but just throw these amendments, sometimes in technical terms, at the house just at the moment the clause to which they relate is called in committee of the whole.

The Minister of Finance has chosen to be rather nasty in this respect. I complimented the minister fully when I found that he was introducing a system of indicating his changes of mind from budget night before the time we would have a chance of debating the budget issues. I complimented the minister upon the fact that on May 6 he introduced as an appendix to Votes and Proceedings notice of amendments indicating his change of mind since March 31, when he introduced his budget, and in so doing gave notice to those affected as taxpayers of his intention to move these amendments.
What I complained about and continue to complain about is that the minister did not continue the good job in this respect. Why did he not, between May 6 and now, bring in this two-page amendment; because the public at large has not the same kind of
Income Tax Act
advantage with regard to notice that we have. I praised the minister for introducing the amendments on May 6.
The minister has suggested that I asked on a certain date-was it June 13?-that the debate on second reading not be proceeded with. I want to say to the House of Commons, and to the country at large, that I quoted to the minister over the telephone a letter I received from the people in this land chiefly responsible for examining income tax matters, the Canadian tax foundation, in which they said it would be an affront to them and to the taxpayers at large if the minister and the leader of the house on the government side proposed to go ahead on Monday with the debate on second reading, because the public at large would not have had an opportunity of considering the debate that had taken place the preceding week.
The Canadian tax foundation had an appointment-now, I want the Minister of Finance to deny this if it is not so, since he has brought my name into this discussion by saying that I asked for delay-with the officials of his department in the subsequent week. What the minister and the government were proposing was that, prior to that appointment, we would be asked in this house to give second reading to this bill without the consultation which the Canadian tax foundation had informally every year with the officials of the department.
I do not want the Minister of Finance to say, Mr. Chairman, that I asked for postponement of the debate on second reading. I found that the leader of the house, on that particular Friday night, did indicate that the subject would not be debated on the following Monday. My request was on behalf of those experts who wanted to analyse the bill which had been presented only a few days before.

speechtext: I understand we are dealing with clause 3 as amended. The new subsection (5b)-I am speaking now of the original clause 3 of the bill, owing to the fact that the amendment has now been carried and disposed of-is explained in the printed explanatory note. The regulations prescribed under the authority of the Income Tax Act provide for rates of capital cost allowance or depreciation that may be claimed by taxpayers. These regulations divide depreciable assets into about 18 classes, with a different rate for each class. It sometimes happens that a taxpayer regards some asset as falling in a class which enjoys a lower rate of allowance than that for which it properly qualifies and that when he finds his error he will wish to transfer the property to its proper class. It may also happen that the minister will find that a taxpayer has regarded his assets as qualifying for a higher rate of allowance than that to which they are entitled, and the minister will direct that the asset be transferred to its proper class. The amendment made in clause 3 will provide rules to be followed in this event.

When the house rose for the luncheon recess order No. 7, dealing with the appointment of a select committee on broadcasting, had been called. It is not my purpose at the moment to make any extended remarks whatsoever on this matter. This motion arises out of the hearings of the committee last year. At the conclusion of those hearings an understanding was arrived at that a similar committee would be set up during this session.
I can anticipate some criticism to the effect that the committee should have been set up earlier, and so on and so forth. I shall be prepared at least to consider those arguments if, as and when they are presented to this house. At the moment all I wish to say is that this committee is being set up now and that the terms of reference are slightly different from those of the committee of last year, but I think only in detail, not in principle.
Last year the committee was set up to deal exclusively with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I am advised by the law officers of the department and of the House of Commons that this resolution meets that requirement, and that in addition to the reference to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation there is included the Canadian association of broadcasters, or in other words the private broadcasters of Canada, and also

the board of broadcast governors. I think the committee last year expressed the opinion that at the next session they should have an opportunity to consider the work of the board of broadcast governors as well as the opinions of the C.A.B. Other than that, this motion is exactly the same as the motion which has been presented to this house throughout the years.
I do not think any good purpose would be served by my making any extensive remarks at this time, although at the conclusion of the debate, if there is one, I shall be glad to deal with any matters which are raised.

Mr. Speaker, I hope there will not be any extended debate on this motion, for this reason. I am going to suggest to the minister -and I might as well make the suggestion right at the outset-that at the conclusion of such debate as there may be he seek leave of the house to withdraw this motion. To introduce this motion at this stage of this session of parliament, unless it is intended to adjourn parliament next week and come back in September or October-in which case I think it would be more sensible to wait until September or October to introduce the motion-is making a mockery of parliament.
In support of that statement I think perhaps I could read no greater authority than the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), the Minister of National Revenue, speaking in this house on August 25, 1958 at a good deal earlier stage of the session of 1958 than we have now reached in the session of 1960. On August 25, 1958 we had not sat for as many days as we have now been sitting in this session. At that time, speaking about a proposal that had appeared in the speech from the throne at the beginning of that session, the minister said he thought it was too late to appoint a committee which could do anything useful. Here are his exact words, which are to be found at page 4045 of Hansard of August 25, 1958:
As far as the regulations are concerned-
That is to say, the regulations which would be made under the Broadcasting Act which was then under consideration in the house.
-they are to be promulgated by the board itself, and neither I nor anyone else can say, except in very broad outline, what they are going to be. I certainly echo that hope.

I think I could echo that hope also.
-and that the government will then be dealing with the backlog of matters-
I think it is about time they started dealing with the backlog of matters today.
-which hon. gentlemen know always accumulate during a session. Then it will give consideration to the personnel of these two boards.

On behalf of the government, Mr. Speaker, I would say-

On behalf of the government, Mr. Speaker, I would say that if it is requested at the next session of parliament, we will shortly after the session begins set up a special committee of the house to deal with radio and broadcasting generally. All these matters can be referred to that committee, and perhaps the committee can watch the organization take shape and form and grow during the session rather than speculate, which is all we can do now concerning the operation of the bill.
I took that statement then, as I take it still, to be an undertaking on the part of the government. This matter came up for discussion on a number of other occasions, as the hon. gentleman will recall, when the view taken on this side of the house was that we wanted to have a committee which would not go on fishing expeditions in all sorts of quarters but would have specific terms of reference and would address itself to consideration of the operation of the broadcasting legislation which the hon. gentleman was then piloting through the house.
We in the Liberal opposition took the very strongest exception to certain features of that broadoasting legislation. In forgoing at the request of the hon. gentleman a right which we would have had to have that legislation considered in committee, to have witnesses called, and so on, we always understood that we were to have a committee on the legislation and its operation. But instead of that, when we did get a committee last year we had a committee that turned itself into a kind of super board of governors of the C.B.C. and started to niggle about all kinds of little things about which most members of this house have no real knowledge and no competence to discuss, seeking to supplant the board which parliament had appointed under its legislation-legislation of which we did not entirely approve-for the purpose of regulating broadcasting.
Broadcasting
We do not think any useful purpose at all would be served by that kind of committee. What we want is a committee that will consider the principles on which the broadcasting legislation is based and on which broadcasting operates in this country, and we want to consider them in a reasonable and systematic manner.
That there is need for such a committee I do not for one minute deny, and I want to give one or two illustrations of the kind of thing into which I think there is some need for a committee to look. But before I do that I want to say why we do not think this committee should be set up at this stage of the session.
We do not think it should be set up at this stage of the session because it is utterly impossible for those members of the opposition-and I speak only for my own colleagues in the opposition because other members of the opposition will speak for themselves-who are greatly interested in the subject of broadcasting to do their duty in this house and their duty in one or two other committees which are of the utmost importance, particularly in the banking and commerce committee which is sitting at this very moment and where I ought to be if I did not have to be here.

But we do know as a matter of fact that on both sides of the house there are certain people who have certain interests, and we know that there is legislation before this parliament which has to be considered by committees if the legislation is going to be dealt with at all.
There will be nothing before this committee except the general subject of broadcasting, and the general subject of broadcasting has not changed to any appreciable degree since last January. There is no reason why this committee could not have been set up at latest by February 1, and could not have had its meetings at a time when there was no legislation to be considered and when those members who had devoted some study to the matter and are especially interested in it would have had ample opportunity to give the kind of consideration to the committee which ought to be given a subject of this importance.

Broadcasting
As I say, at this stage I am not going to do more than appeal to the minister to get the consent of the house at the end of this debate to withdraw this motion and give us an undertaking that as the first item of ordinary business at the next session a similar motion will be made. I think it would be preferable if the government would give consideration to an amendment of the standing orders to make the broadcasting committee a standing committee of the house. I have been in government, and I know what an embarrassment it is to find time for a debate such as we are engaged in now.
Perhaps I should not say anything in extenuation of the government, but I know it is sometimes difficult jockeying for position to get things on. It is often said that a certain debate will take a whole day and that that is a day lost and a motion gets put off from week to week and then from month to month, as this motion did. Of course it was not on the order paper for very long; it was only put on the order paper on May 30, but it might have been put on in January and still have been in much the same position. I feel that at this stage of the session we should not be put in this kind of position at all.
The other thing is that I appeal to the minister to do what in 1958 he certainly gave us in the opposition the impression he was going to do, namely to introduce a motion in express terms so the terms of reference of that committee will deal with the Broadcasting Act and the operations of the act itself, instead of permitting these general investigations into this, that and the other thing connected with the detailed operations of broadcasting. I am not saying that if hon. members do not want to do that they should be denied the opportunity; not at all; but I do think a prior commitment was given to the opposition by the government which I maintain has not been kept and which I think should be kept. That is the argument I am making.
I am not arguing that this committee should not be set up because an investigation is not needed. An investigation is needed, but it does seem to me that, at this stage of the session, the only appropriate way in which we can carry on a discussion on broadcasting at all is in committee of supply, when the estimates come before us. I might say that is one reason why this whole situation is different from what it was in the past. In the past, up until 1956, there were no estimates of the C.B.C. and no broadcasting estimates. The C.B.C. was provided with a budget in another way, and the only opportunity for any discussion of broadcasting was in a committee. But now, owing to a regrettable step

taken by the present government, a step which we intend to change when we get into office, there is an annual budget for the C.B.C. which keeps the C.B.C. pretty effectively under the thumb under the Minister of Finance.
That is a principle in which we do not believe. It is a principle which leads in the direction of totalitarianism. We believe that the C.B.C. and the whole broadcasting set-up in Canada should have the same kind of independence the judiciary has. That is the only safe way to have broadcasting by the state.

We believe, and we have always believed, that the state-operated broadcasting system should be subject to parliament and not to the government. This was spelled out carefully in the Massey commission report. There is something I do know something about, and it is this. Under this legislation a certain obligation was placed upon the president and the vice president of the C.B.C. and last year, as the hon. gentleman will recall, certain questions were asked in this house about certain regrettable things that happened at a time when the president of the corporation was absent. Then later the vice president, on account of the stress and strain of certain circumstances, also had to be absent.
I asked the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), who was then in the government and was the acting minister, to tell us who was presiding over the board of the C.B.C. The hon. member took my question as notice, and subsequently the present minister gave an answer to the question as will be found on page 5777 of Hansard of July 10, 1959. Perhaps it would be convenient to put both the question and the answer on record:

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RADIO AND TELEVISION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could put a question to the Minister of National Revenue. Could the minister tell us who at the present time is performing the statutory functions of the president of the C.B.C. as chairman of the board of directors?

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RADIO AND TELEVISION
speechtext:
Colonel Landry is, as I said, chairman of the management committee, and Mr. Dunsmore is chairman of the executive committee of the board of directors and the absence of the vice president is acting as chairman of the board.
It cannot be said that the question took the minister by surprise, because he had been given notice of it. One would have thought that in circumstances such as these, when a question of this importance was being asked, the minister would have fortified himself with all the available information. Yet after parliament had adjourned, in fact after the session had been prorogued, an announcement was made that Mr. Dunsmore had been appointed chairman of the board. I have here a news item from the Gazette of August 18, 1959 which reads "Dunsmore is named C.B.C. board head." The text is as follows:
Robert L. Dunsmore, retired oil company head and former president of the Montreal board of

Broadcasting
trade has been named chairman of the C.B.C. board of directors, it was announced yesterday.
On subsequent inquiries being made it turned out-I have all the documents here, but I do not wish to weary the house by going into the details-it turned out that Mr. Dunsmore was elected to be chairman of the board at a meeting on June 23 or 24. This transaction apparently had been kept secret from the minister, or at least the minister said nobody ever told him about it. Then, after parliament had adjourned, this information was ferreted out by the press, who were apparently more successful than I had been by asking a direct question here in parliament. It seems to me that even had there been no question about the legality of this whole performance it was a very shabby way to treat parliament or any member of parliament asking questions about public business in such an important sphere as this. But I have the very greatest doubt about the legality of this whole transaction.

speechtext:
I assure Your Honour that you are under a grave misapprehension, because if the government persists and does establish a committee of the kind proposed, this matter will certainly be discussed in that committee. I say this notwithstanding the fact that it might be an argument for not discussing it here and now.
What I should like to point out to Your Honour is that I am seeking to persuade the minister not to proceed with this motion at the present time. I am seeking to persuade the minister that when he makes the motion at the next session of parliament he should make the kind of motion which will enable us to come to grips with these things that

really matter; that is to say, with the fundamentals of the broadcasting legislation. I am suggesting that the C.B.C. board of governors, under the law as it now stands, had no power to substitute anyone, except in an emergency and for an emergency period, for a temporary period, for the president in his capacity as chairman of the board.
If one examines the debates-and I do not intend to go into details on this; I shall do that on the estimates-if one examines the exchanges that took place on this precise point during the debate on the bill he will find it is perfectly clear that parliament never contemplated-and if the government contemplated it they were misleading parliament -at the time that legislation went through that in this clandestine manner someone would be substituted for the president of the C.B.C. as chairman of the board. Certainly I have nothing to say in a personal way about Mr. Dunsmore one way or another. He may be an altogether more suitable person to be the chairman of the board than the president. That is not the point at issue. What I am saying is that parliament enacted a certain law and something else is being done, and it is certainly something that should not be permitted to continue.
I also wish to say it seems to me that one of the other fundamental matters that ought to be considered by a committee is the whole new question of the criteria for the granting of licences to private television stations in places where the C.B.C. also is, and the duplication as well by the C.B.C. of stations in places now served by private television. Hon. members know, because I have asked questions and expressed views about it, that I regard it as an unnecessary waste of the taxpayers' money to have a public television station established in the city of Edmonton, which is very well served at the present time by a private station, when there are all kinds of outlying points like places in Newfoundland and northern Manitoba,-

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RADIO AND TELEVISION
speechtext: And in northern Ontario.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RADIO AND TELEVISION
speechtext:
-and in northern Ontario which are not served, though I have no doubt the hon. member for Port Arthur will have something to say about that. I feel that this kind of extension, this use of public funds to extend television coverage in areas already adequately covered, when there are a great many parts of Canada that have no coverage, indicates a very mistaken idea of priority.
I also feel that we need some explanation of the care with which the board of broadcast governors appeared to follow what I believe everyone thought was the established

principle that, while no place should be denied television coverage because no one except the local newspaper or a corporation largely owned by that newspaper would provide it, in places where there were other applicants equally worthy and equally competent it was undesirable as a matter of public policy, frequently expressed on both sides of this house, that newspapers or organizations closely allied with newspapers should be preferred to other applicants. It is very hard now to understand this extraordinary decision which was made in Toronto in favour of a newspaper whose proprietor, according to all reports, months before the application was heard by the board went about saying that there was no need for them to hold any hearing because he already had it. It does seem to me that is something which needs very careful investigation, as well as the whole policy underlying that situation.
I might say in that context, sir, that the same newspaper apparently has a great deal of worry, because it has spent a lot of time trying to misrepresent what has been said in criticism of the decision in this matter.
I do hope that before the minister approves this Edmonton television station, unless the governor in council has approved it already, the estimates will be brought forward and we shall be given an opportunity to discuss the wisdom of that move.
It does seem to me, sir, that I should go back to my original and fundamental point and not take more of the time of the house on other matters. As I say, we feel that a committee is desirable; we feel that there should be a committee every year; we feel that the most advisable way of dealing with this matter from the point of view of saving the time of the house would be to have a standing committee so that it would be just set up in the same way as the other standing committees and the time of the house saved in those circumstances. But we do not feel that a committee set up on the 107th day of the session can possibly be expected, in view of all the demands upon our time both in the house and in other committees where it is essential for members to be present if they are to do their duty properly, to do the work that requires to be done. We do not think it is the appropriate thing to do at all.
I appeal to the minister to give us an undertaking that the committee will be set up early in the next session, and to withdraw this motion. However, if the minister is not willing to accede to this appeal-and I hope he will indicate what his intentions are one way or the other before he speaks
Broadcasting
in closing the debate-I think we are entitled to be told so by someone from the government side at an early stage; because if that does happen we intend, in order to test the house, to move that this motion be read this day six months hence. But I do not wish to do that unless the minister cares to say one way or the other right now what his intentions are. I would prefer to leave it to the minister to withdraw the motion.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RADIO AND TELEVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult for me and my colleagues to be belligerent, but it is very hard for us to do other than react rather badly to this particular motion at this particular time. We feel that it is a bad time in the session to be bringing it in. It would be different, we feel, if we could contemplate the session moving rather slowly toward an end some time in September, but we are already under a certain amount of forced draft and we are likely to be forced even further in so far as the extension of hours is concerned.
There are a great number of committees meeting. The previous speaker referred to that fact. I was bothered by the interjection from one of the Conservative members challenging the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that there are 48 other Liberals. We have had this challenge thrown, not only to the Liberals but to our very small group, a number of times by the Prime Minister and by other people that we need to learn to spread the work around and we should not expect any special privileges because we are in the opposition. It is not a case of expecting special privileges, but I think the government members, and especially the senior government members, should realize-I know that the veterans know it- that there is a difference in the roles that opposition members and government members play in much of the work here.
Quite frankly, we cannot give the attention that this committee deserves if it is set up and gets under way. That being the case, we can only feel that it is bad to set up the committee. If the Conservative members feel that with their great strength they can man the committee and do the job, they are entitled to believe that; but I think they have to recognize that the opposition should be playing some role.
I want to make some specific references to the committee of last year. I should like to point out to the minister that the members of that committee from the government side who made the greatest contribution in terms of cross-examination and good attendance, and who were the key people in preparing the report, are all involved in activities that

Broadcasting
will make it very difficult tor them to take part in the work of the committee this year. The chairman is already involved as chairman of another committee this session. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell), who played a large role in the committee, is now parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance and is also taking part in other committees. The hon. member who is parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Defence was very active in the committee last year, and we gather that he has his work cut out for him now in his departmental role. I could go right down the list of members who played an active part in that committee, which might be an invidious thing to do, and point out that all of them, both opposition and government members, are actively involved either in other committees or in extended commitments they did not have last summer.
It seems to me that this supports the logic that the government should withdraw this motion and give us an undertaking that the committee will be set up early in the next session. To argue this way is not to argue that there is not a great deal of work for a committee to do. The aftermaths of last summer still linger. I think the most unfortunate one, and I cannot articulate it in this debate, is that there has been a terrible effect upon the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I think the programming situation has gone to the dogs. In my opinion there is a gutlessness in the organization which is amazing and most regrettable.
I think we could very well spend a great deal of time in this committee, if we had the time, trying to encourage and develop a completely new approach on the part of parliament and the government. I do not know how the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate manages to separate them so neatly. It seems to me we need a new approach as to what the role of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is going to be. As commercialism has been extended this year in an effort to make more money, partly as a result of the committee's recommendation, it seems to me we are getting more and more vacuity and a poorer and poorer job in public affairs.
For example, I think that the coverage the C.B.C. has given recent Canadian political affairs involving provincial elections is ridiculous. If you turn on the radio at any time you can hear about Khrushchev or Castro or Nasser, but apparently the C.B.C. feels that where people like Stanfield, Hicks, Douglas and Thatcher are concerned it will get into hot water if it gives them any kind of decent coverage. I sometimes wonder how we are going to get a Canadian nationality through

the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation when it seems to concentrate most of its public affairs programs upon foreign affairs, and I say that without any regret at all. Surely there is enough of interest in our own country to give this organization something to do. But its objectives in that field are falling farther and farther away from the mark. I think they are scared stiff to do some decent programming relating to Canadian issues in the public affairs field. They are scared stiff partly because of the incidents of last summer in which the broadcasting committee was involved.
I think the board of broadcast governors has everyone up in the air. I have here the lovely correspondence which the Globe and Mail published as a result of the decision to give the Telegram the television licence in Toronto. I have heard that it was solicited, but whether or not it was solicited it is a magnificent collection of letters, especially starting with the one by Joseph Sedgwick, Q.C., whom we all know was an interested party, entitled by the paper "The Curtain Falls". I think we all appreciated the touch of poetry in the last part of the letter, where these words were used:
'Ere they hewed the Sphinx's visage Favoritism governed kissage,
Even as it does in this age And it will do evermore.
The general reaction to the award of that particular licence to the Telegram and Mr. Aldred and the others associated with him was, I think, the most vivid indication of disappointment in the board of broadcast governors that one could imagine. At one stroke it seemed to undo everything toward which the board of broadcast governors was moving, and it is still unfathomable to me and to many others. Before the award was made there was a great deal of speculation around the House of Commons. A number of us had our No. 1, No. 2 and No. 3 predictions, and invariably for a whole host of reasons the bottom one in the order was the Telegram entry. Yet the Telegram got the licence.
When the board of broadcast governors turned their backs upon the Siftons in Winnipeg we seemed to have an indication that newspapers were not going to be given these licences, but then we got the Telegram. I think it is generally agreed by people who follow newspapers that you have to go a long waj and search extensively to find a metropolitan daily as bad in almost every way as the Toronto Telegram. If the standards of the Toronto Telegram are going to be transferred to the television station all I can say is, God help the Toronto listeners and watchers. I have no brief, and I do not think anyone in this

party has, for the Toronto Globe and Mail, but better the Globe and Mail a thousand times than the Telegram.

One of the matters that has bothered me about the C.B.C. is the tendency to weasel ever since the broadcasting committee sat last year. I want to give an example of this, and it relates to an answer that was given to me through the minister reporting for the C.B.C. Last February I had a question on the order paper, and it was this:
At the meeting of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation board of directors in January at Winnipeg did one of the directors make a statement or a report, verbal or written, on audience reaction to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation programming?
What I had in mind was the well known Mrs. Aitken and her campaign to develop several thousand program critics across the country. The second question was:
If so, which director and in what form was the report?
Was this report prepared by the director in person or was it prepared in co-operation with officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation?
If the latter, what officials in which branch of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation?
I should like to ask you to pay attention to this doozer of an answer I got, Mr. Speaker. The answer was as follows:
-I am advised by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that minutes and proceedings of the board of directors of the corporation have always been regarded as confidential,-
This is a laugh, because that report was spread all over the Winnipeg Free Press and all over the Winnipeg Tribune.
*-and this has been recognized since the inception of the corporation. Names of individuals involved in the business of the corporation have also been regarded as confidential, a practice reaffirmed by the 1959 parliamentary committee on broadcasting.
Yet the minister and others know that in the report that was splattered all over the newspapers Mrs. Aitken said something to the effect that the people of Canada were tired of Foster Hewitt. I have no brief for Foster Hewitt, but what business has she, as the result of her report and her investigation and the subsidized use of C.B.C. personnel, to come out with a report like that? Then we are told by the minister answering for the C.B.C. that this had nothing to do with it at all. Surely when Mrs. Aitken goes to Winnipeg to a meeting of the C.B.C. she is going in a public capacity, and the statements she makes there in regard to her investigations are something relating to the C.B.C. board of directors. The answer the minister gave ended in this way:
Consequently it is not considered in the best interests of the corporation to depart from that practice at this time.

This is nothing but weaseling in not giving an honest or direct answer. I say we are aware that the corporation, through one of its branches, has spent a great deal of time and a great deal of money trying to cooperate with Mrs. Aitken on her audience research survey, this plan of hers to tap the ladies and other people who follow radio and television closely across the country. The result, as revealed in that answer, would tend to be a complete denial that this great big splurge that Mrs. Aitken made in Winnipeg has any substance at all.
This is not the way I understand it, and in my opinion it is another example of the fact that there was a hot potato issue here. I do not believe that this is important. I was just curious as to who gave Mrs. Aitken the right to stand up and sound off about the results of her survey. This is the kind of weasel answer you get instead of a pungent, direct and clear statement. Certainly there is no question about it; we need a much clearer policy on broadcasting and television than we have at the present time.
Issues have been popping up all the time. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate mentioned one, the question of the Edmonton station. I do not know how the members in the cities are affected, but if the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson), the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Beni-dickson), and hon. members representing constituencies in northern Saskatchewan do not have people roosting on their tails all the time about the C.B.C. extending its facilities, then I am very much mistaken. This is one of the biggest issues in this part of the country.
What do they find? They find the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation putting up $300,000 to telecast football games. This is fine, and nobody will disagree with it. However, what about the prime responsibility of the corporation to give everyone in Canada service? We check up on the C.B.C. as to its future plans and find one of the most hesitant, backward, mystifying policies one could find in relation to extending their television service in this country. There is no policy at all that I can see. When you do investigate you are given a lot of figures about so many dollars per head, so many dollars per household.
The people in Churchill, in Flin Flon, in the northern part of Port Arthur, in Kenora-Rainy River, in northern New Brunswick and in these places do not want to hear about the cost per head when the C.B.C. is spending $300,000 on football or opening a station in Edmonton for additional coverage. They want to know when they are going to get some television service. If it is not up to those who are on the treasury board, the

Minister of Finance or the minister responsible for this organization to do something, then I do not know where we are going to get the answer.
I had some hope when the board of broadcast governors was appointed that they would give a lead. It seems to me they have been stalling. There are no indications that they are taking this whole question of hinterland development into consideration at all.
Another matter that has come to the fore, it seems to me, is connected with the purchase of this North Bay station by the Thomson interests. It has not been ratified as yet by the board, but I suppose it is going to be considered. Surely they are in a position to decide, yes or no, whether we are going to have a continued build-up of these large corporate aggregations in the communications field.
Now, it seems to me that the Winnipeg decision which gave the Siftons a kick in the teeth-I do not believe the Siftons expected to get anything but a kick in the teeth-led us to believe that we were on our way. We were going to have no control by newspapers in the radio and television field; there was going to be a check on what had been a long-standing trend, but the Telegram case just reversed that.
Now we have Thomson spreading his empire in many parts of the empire, if I can put it that way. He is coming back into television in the manner on which we need a ruling and a decision fairly soon. No matter what the individual enterprise of a person who has a television licence or a station, there is no question that if someone offers a big enough price he will sell it. We can see that trend with the truckers who come down here bucking the C.N.R. They go into trucking and then they turn around the next day and sell out to the C.N.R. If Mr. Thomson gathers all the capital that has been offered to him over in Britain and comes back here I am sure he can wind up by buying almost every television station in Canada. It seems to me that we are at the stage where we need some kind of indication from the B.B.G., the government or some kind of public discussion as to how far this aggregating in television and radio should be allowed to go and the whole relationship of the press with the field.
I think we all noticed the sounding off done by Senator Rupert Davies over in England the other day when he came out with remarks that indicated that he had a low opinion of the board of broadcast governors and the harmful effect these decisions are going to have on broadcasting in Canada. I should like to point out to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that the senator is a Liberal, and 79951-0-328

It is a Liberal principle and I offer it not only to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate but to Senator Davies.
The fundamental question underlying the difficulties of television and broadcasting today in terms of policy stem from the reorientation the government gave to the long standing tradition that went back to the 1930's when it decided to encourage the C.B.C. to commercialize and to grant television licences. I am not the kind of socialist who is going to stand howling about the government making this decision. When you are

Broadcasting
faced with a government decision and a policy that sets us off on another line, while you may be critical of it, you must go along to the extent of trying to see that it works in the best way possible.
However, I now wonder whether we have not reached the stage where we have confusion compounded as a result of the two authorities, namely the B.B.G. and the C.B.C. and as a result of the private interests who are now in the television field. For the life of me I cannot see what we are going to get out of it in terms of what we used to expect from our broadcasting policies, namely some kind of dike or protection from United States cultural influences and some means of bringing national coverage-and I emphasize "national coverage"-to every part of the country. It seems to me that there are holes and pitfalls all over in so far as that policy is concerned as a result of recent developments.
In summing up, may I say that we think there is a great deal for a broadcasting committee to do, but we do not think this is the time or the occasion for it unless we can have the assurance that the government does not plan to extend the hours of the sittings but that it plans to take its time and probably to go on to mid-August or the first of September. In that case, with that length of time available it seems to me that by working slowly, with perhaps one meeting a week, the committee might do some kind of job. In any other circumstances it would be impracticable. I should still like to hear from the minister how he is going to man this committee from the government benches in terms of those people who were so active in the committee last year and who have so many other commitments this year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be extremely brief. I wish to express a view altogether different from the argument advanced by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), who said it is questionable whether the committee on broadcasting should sit at every session. This year that committee has yet to sit. That committee was formed not because of a whim of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), or of the government, or even of parliament. It is merely the result of a justifiable wish of the general public.
Last year, the committee performed a task that was difficult, I admit, but a useful one,

since there has been a noticeable improvement in the C.B.C. Unfortunately, the improvement noted is not proportionate to the amount of work done by the committee.
I realize that we are now pretty late in this session. The pleasant summer months are starting, but the vital importance and urgent necessity of this committee certainly does not justify the objections being made today against its establishment.
In the first place, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate stated earlier that the C.B.C. should be as independent as the judiciary. If I am mistaken, I know he will correct me, but I believe that is what he said.
The C.B.C. is called upon to spend each year from $50 million to $100 million of taxpayers' money. Parliament is therefore justified in calling the C.B.C. to account for its administration. The public asks for it, the public demands it.
Moreover, even if last year, during committee proceedings we were often accused of partisanship, the number of letters received by committee members and other members of the house, together with the many comments reported in the press, not to mention what we were told by people of all political allegiances and of all schools of thought, all show that everybody readily approved of the work performed by the committee and asked, in fact, that it be carried on this year.
I am one of those who believe that the C.B.C. must enjoy a certain degree of independence. On the other hand, I also believe that this independence is no justification for extravagance or unwarranted expenditures that are even frowned upon by taxpayers.
I believe that in the matter of programming and expenditures, the C.B.C. should be given the free hand it needs for the proper management of its business. I believe, however, that a parliament of representatives elected by those who are paying to insure the efficient operation of the C.B.C. should nevertheless retain some control and ask the corporation for some account of its activity and management. As a matter of fact, it has been said over and again: "For an administration, the fear of parliament is the beginning of wisdom." The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) said earlier-in what seemed to me the strongest of his arguments-that since the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) is now parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, the committee could not

possibly be efficient. He mentioned the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Chambers) and a few others. Now, I believe that, if the committee were to sit next September or January, those gentlemen would not be able to attend it either because I have a feeling that next year, they will be holding the same, if not higher, responsibilities.
That is why I must say that Conservative members of parliament are inclined to take up their work again this year, and are ready to co-operate to every possible extent in order to continue an inquiry started last year which had already begun to bear fruit and to give the committee a little more latitude than last year. People expect us to go on with this inquiry to obtain any information they are entitled to get.
Mr. Speaker, previous speakers listed a series of radio and television stations that have been granted licences. By a strange coincidence, it seemed that all those licences had been delivered to people whose political affiliation was not their own, which they seem-to think extraordinary.
May I recall your attention to that point, Mr. Speaker, and tell you that, before the present administration came into power, licences were delivered, for instance, to station CFCM-TV and to station CKMI-TV owned by Messrs. Picard and Bray, people of known Liberal affiliations.
There is also station CJBR-TV in Rimouski, owned by Mr. Brillant, a Liberal member of the legislative council, Station CKBL, in Matane, is also operated by the same owner. In fact every television station in Quebec is operated under a licence granted by the former government, and is owned by Liberals. Talking of coincidences, the cases I have just mentioned are a rather striking example.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, let me say that if the investigation of the C.B.C. is to be continued, I feel sure that every hon. member will want to take part in the discussions of the committee that is to be set up, and do so in a very objective way. Quite obviously, we are not trying to make political hay. We, in Quebec are just winding up an election campaign, and I think if the committee had been sitting, it would have provided an opportunity for a certain amount of election talk; however, we are pleased that the committee will not be sitting until after the election. Thus, no one will be able to accuse us of trying to make political hay.
We are taking a completely objective attitude. We want to throw some light on the C.B.C. because I must say-and this will be 79951-0-328J
Broadcasting
my last word-that in the province of Quebec people are justly alarmed and concerned over the way a group of individuals are spending the taxpayers' money at the rate of over $50 million a year, without having to account for it to any authority.

Mr. Speaker, I happen to have before me Votes and Proceedings for the last week. I cannot begin to pick out those which are more important than others, but there are certainly four, if not five, of these which are of extreme importance where all of us sitting on both sides of the house who want to do our duty feel it is necessary to be present.
The next day, Tuesday, June 14, appears in' Votes and Proceedings notices for the sittings of seven committees, several of which are important.

The Votes and Proceedings for Monday of this week, that is yesterday, indicates that notices were sent out of meetings, which ostensibly took place, for nine committees, the vast majority being of importance.

Broadcasting
Now the minister seeks to set up a select committee on broadcasting to deal with a matter which when it was last submitted took many weeks, in fact months, to dispose of the matters which came before it.
I do not know what is in the mind of the house leader but I have some idea that if it is the intention of the government to complete the sittings of this session on one of these days in the not too far off future he will move to take away from us the lunch hour. will have to give some thought to those who are to appear before the committee; whether the board of broadcast governors are to appear first, whether the independent broadcasting associations are to be called next, and things of that nature, and if, as I said earlier, it is the intention of the government to take away the lunch hour then our position will be an impossible one. Order. May I interrupt the hon. member to say a few words about the amendment. It has been brought to my attention that citation 202, paragraph 11, of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, reads as follows:
An amendment proposing that a resolution which does not require second reading be considered this day six months is out of order.

I was quite aware of the citation to which you refer; in fact, I had it in my hand when the motion was drawn, and I wish to direct to your attention the fact that there are two points which I think differentiate it from the paragraph in question. Subparagraph 11 of citation 202 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, at page 170, says that:
An amendment proposing that a resolution which does not require second reading be considered this day six months is out of order.
You will note, first of all, that this amendment is for a period of eight months, which would bring it to the month of February of next year, when the next session would normally be sitting and which perhaps would be a more appropriate time than now.
The other point is that our amendment asks that the committee be appointed eight months hence and not this day six months, which is the practice in ordinary motions, which I believe is covered by subparagraph 11, so that it seems to me that these two differentials indicate that the motion is in order.

Mr. Speaker, with respect I think that the arguments of the hon. member for Laurier are not applicable. There is,

surely, only one type of amendment known as a dilatory amendment. The standard form is, of course, six months. I believe that sometimes they have been drawn in the form of three months. It seems to me I have seen reference to the form "three months or six months hence". Whether or not one varies the figure any number of months between three, six, eight, nine and twelve, that form of the amendment and the effect of the amendment are the same and it falls, therefore, within the same category as that described in paragraph 11 of citation 202 to which you have referred.
The effect of the amendment would be to give the motion an eight months hoist and it is therefore, I submit, exactly in the same category as those described in the citation.
There is another point that I would like to raise, however, because of the argument made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). He said the effect of the amendment would be to require the appointment of the committee in February next when, as he said, with what prescience I do not know, the house would be again in session. I point out to you, sir, that that would surely be another session and it is a well established rule, as I recall it, that orders of the house applicable or made in one session are not applicable to another session unless they be readopted at the other session. Therefore, the effect of the prorogation of this session would be to destroy or cancel the order. Therefore accepting the argument of the hon. member that the desire of his amendment is to postpone the appointment of the committee to February next, that purpose is not achieved because of the fact that he himself has drawn to our attention, and indeed, in whichever category he wants to put his amendment, the effect is simply that of a straight negative thereby defeating the motion. Therefore, I submit to you, sir, that the citation has application and the amendment is out of order.

May I say a word, sir. I agree with the Minister of Justice that whether the motion said six months or eight months is not relevant; what is relevant is that this is not such a motion at all. My hon. friend's amendment is not a motion at all to defer the consideration or the decision of the house; it is a motion to amend a resolution before the house by inserting into that resolution the words "that a select committee be appointed this day eight months". It is not a motion to defer a decision. If this amendment were passed it would be a declaration of the house that the resolution was accepted; whereas the six months hoist is a motion that

something be not read now, or be not adopted now, but be adopted six months later which is an entirely different thing.
As for the subsidiary matter raised by the Minister of Justice, the factor of the secrets of the future, of course, his judgment is a little better than ours because he has perhaps a little more to say about when the session will end or, at least, when it will begin, but we do not know that. But we do not know whether this same session may not be going on next February. In the memory of some members, including the Prime Minister, who were in the house at the time, it did happen that a session started on November 7, 1940 and, if my recollection is accurate, it was not prorogued until some time in January of 1942. Therefore it could very well happen. It certainly is not for the Chair but rather for the house to decide whether or not a motion which says that something should be done eight months hence would in fact be capable of being carried out. If members of the house do not think it is a sensible thing to adopt, they can of course defeat it, but it would appear to be a very arbitrary thing for the Chair to decide that.
I submit that what my hon. friend has asked the house to decide in this amendment, which provides that a select committee on broadcasting be appointed this day eight months hence and so on and so forth, is an amendment of the proposition itself and not in any sense an attempt to defer a decision on the motion. It is certainly not a negative.

On a question of privilege, I believe I was speaking at the time of the interruption and if I do not proceed now I may be told I have made my remarks and have no right to speak again. It is only on that ground that I dare interfere with the

hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) . I was mentioning that I find myself in a somewhat difficult position in this matter, as a member of parliament very often does.
I Was impressed with the remarks of previous speakers that, having regard to the importance of the terms of reference, it might be that a very poor job would be done by this committee that would not be in the best interests of the C.B.C. or the people of Canada if the committee were to sit at this stage of the session when so many other committees are meeting. I would be quite prepared to support these contentions if it were not for one thing. I have not been able to get an answer from the minister with respect to whether there is any intention to bring in any changes to the act governing the C.B.C. at this session. If it is the intention of the minister or the government to bring in changes this session, particularly with respect to one matter, I would be quite satisfied to sit down but so far I have not been able to get any assurance either by word of mouth or in writing. Therefore I have to raise a matter which I do not like to raise. However, I feel that I must do so, although it does not concern me personally at all.
It is a matter which in my opinion is of such importance that if the minister is not going to deal with it voluntarily then it should be considered by the committee to be appointed under this motion so that a recommendation can be made to the minister and the government for action to be taken at this session. I am not trying to keep members in suspense. The matter I have in mind concerns all members of the House of Commons generally and a number in particular. I believe it has to be dealt with and should be dealt with by a committee now.
As a result of my study of the situation and according to the best information I can get from top calibre legal counsel outside of the house and also from the Department of Justice it would appear to me that prior to the present parliament some members sat in their places illegally and there may be some who, unconsciously and unintentionally, are sitting in the house illegally at the present time under the wording of two acts affecting the House of Commons.
I drew this matter to the attention of the Department of Justice on January 20 this year so there has been plenty of notice. I did not know about this matter before and I am certain that nobody else knew about it. I refer to the fact that if a member of the House of Commons or the Senate accepts an invitation to take part in a C.B.C. radio or television broadcast for which an honorarium is paid they do not have the right to sit in the House of Commons. The opinion I have

Broadcasting
received goes even further in that even if the member turns down the honorarium but accepts expenses in connection with attending the radio or television broadcast it is against the law of parliament and he can be challenged on the ground that he is illegally sitting in the house.
To my knowledge hon. members of various parties in previous parliaments have accepted invitations to take part in radio and television broadcasts and have accepted honoraria and expenses. To the best of my information, which comes from a very responsible source, unfortunately there are some members now sitting in the House of Commons who if they have not accepted an honorarium have accepted payment for expenses or have instructed the C.B.C. not to give them the money but to pay it to charity. I do not think the law is evaded in that way. However, that is not the point about which I am so concerned. I almost got into the same situation myself because I accepted an invitation to appear on "Fighting Words" last January. I had to go from Ottawa to Toronto and if I had accepted the honorarium I would have received $100 and also approximately $80 for expenses because I had to fly to Toronto.
For some reason or other something bothered me about the whole matter so I investigated. I inquired not only from high calibre counsel throughout Canada but also in the Department of Justice. I know that the Department of Justice cannot give advice but I received certain information that I think I should give to the house. Anyone who wants it can look it up. This is the information I received:
The statutory provision that has to be considered is section 15 of the Senate and House of Commons Act, K.S.C. 1952, chapter 249, which reads as follows:
No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with any other, by himself or by the interposition of any trustee or third party, holding or enjoying, undertaking or executing any contract or agreement, expressed or implied, with or for the government of Canada on behalf of the crown, or with or for any of the officers of the government of Canada, for which any public money of Canada is to be paid, is eligible as a member of the House of Commons, or shall sit or vote in the said house.
That is the pertinent section from the Senate and House of Commons Act. Then we have subsection 1 of section 4 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, chapter 32, which expressly states:
The corporation is a body corporate having capacity to contract and to sue and be sued in the name of the corporation.
(2) The corporation is for all purposes of this act an agent of Her Majesty and its powers under this act may be exercised only as an agent of Her Majesty.

I am told, therefore, "that it is clear that any arrangement with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation under which the corporation is to pay money falls within the terms of section 15 of the Senate and House of Commons Act. In view of the wording of that section I have difficulty in perceiving any distinction between the payment of a fee or honorarium and the payment of expenses." That is the opinion of the officers of the Department of Justice, and that is the opinion of others on this subject with whom I have consulted outside of the House of Commons. It seems that any member of the House of Commons who accepts any honorarium or payment for expenses from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for appearance on a radio or television program is breaking the law and cannot sit or vote as a member.
As I have said, I drew this to the attention of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which had never warned a member of parliament previously and, in fact, the corporation had not even recognized this fact. I drew it to the attention of the Department of Justice on January 20 because of my concern. It was my understanding, not in writing but verbally, that notice of this would be taken by the government and that in the view of the Department of Justice itself the thing to do was to have an amendment introduced to the Canadian Broadcasting Act. I believe this is of the utmost importance because no member of this house should be placed in a position in which I know hon. members have been placed quite unintentionally by accepting the payment of expenses for travelling to appear on a panel show or something of that nature under the auspices of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I feel it is absolutely essential that if the minister is not concerned at the moment, then the committee must be. This matter must be considered for the protection of the members of the House of Commons, and an amendment must be made for their protection in the future.
I do not believe in a matter of this nature elected members should be paid an honorarium. However, I do believe it should be possible for a member of parliament to attend a radio or television show and not to have to pay his own expenses. There should be a provision whereby a member could accept expenses for attending something of that nature of public interest or national interest. My understanding is, as I have pointed out several times already and confirmed completely by information I have from the Department of Justice, that that is not the present situation.

So, Mr. Speaker, I point out I have only raised this point publicly because I have been waiting now since January 20 and have received no information that any action was going to be taken. I have received no information that the minister now concerned with the department or the Department of Justice had changed their minds on the information they gave me last January. This kind of amendment, therefore, or some other provision is required in the interests of, and for the protection of the members of the House of Commons.
I say, therefore, that if something is going to be done, then I go along with what has been said previously about it being rather late in the session for an important matter like the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to be referred to a special committee. If nothing is going to be done then I feel that in the interests of the House of Commons this committee should be cognizant of this rather dangerous situation because you can never tell when some crank-you know there are always some cranks-might decide to lay charges against a member of the House of Commons as a result of this situation. I say it is unfair that some member of parliament might be caught because he did something unintentionally. In any event, members of parliament now know what the situation is in the opinion of the Department of Justice and others, and they will be very careful in the future. '
