speechtext:
In
view of the wish of the house to have this resolution go the committee as soon as possible, I shall be very brief. I see there is a rather strained look on the minister's face at the present time. I am rising to bring to the attention of the house and urge upon the committee the study of a particular problem.
First of all, like other members, I am sorry that this resolution was not brought before the house earlier this session so that this very important committee would have had more time to deal with the subjects it has to consider. However, I am rising particularly to say a word or two for the people in the hinterlands because I am a hinterlander and I can speak from experience. Do you know that even today there are thousands of people in Canada who have never had the opportunity of enjoying Canadian Broadcasting Corporation programs? These Canadian programs, except in some areas for certain periods during the day and occasionally under certain atmospheric conditions at night, are not available. These people have never had the opportunity of enjoying the programs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on a reliable basis. The areas of which I speak 79951-0-329
Broadcasting
are naturally in the Kootenay district from which I come, the northern part of Kootenay West, some areas in northern British Columbia. I know there are areas in northern Manitoba and northern Ontario, and there may be others.
I do urge that every consideration be given to supplying these people with the necessary low power relay stations that are required to give them at least adequate radio coverage. I know that considerable has been done in recent years, but there is still more to be done. I feel it is most unfair to the people who are living in isolated places, in some cases in mountainous terrain, that they are not able to receive programs from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I do hope that these circumstances, in view of the very large expenditure by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on television, will be rectified so that the people in the hinterland will be able to enjoy this opportunity.
I should like also to make a few references to the same situation which applies with respect to television. There are areas which are affected in exactly the same way because of their location in the mountains. These people today are being denied television of any kind, that is either Canadian or United States television. There is a provision, I understand, providing the regulations of the telecommunications branch of the Department of Transport are met, for persons to instal, after application and acceptance under proper circumstances, a satellite television station.
I have seen one or two in operation. They were most useful. I think in some cases they were called community satellite stations. They are most useful in providing television to those persons beyond the main stream of communication, whether it is radio or television, in certain areas or in areas similar to the ones affected by being unable to receive Canadian radio programs. I urge that every consideration be given to this problem and that those who can provide these services be given an opportunity to do so, in some cases by the formation of crown companies, in other cases co-operatives and in some cases as a result of free enterprise.
Before concluding 1 want to bring one other matter to the attention of the house and it is this. I am of the opinion that at times the C.B.C. takes a somewhat Olympian attitude-and I say that from experience-in not understanding how the people in a certain area or in a certain district are interested in what the C.B.C. intends to do in their district, whether it concerns radio facilities or television facilities. I just want to give an illustration. Over a year ago provision was made for the establishment of a television station to serve the Rossland-Trail area in my

Broadcasting
constituency. Then some unexpected difficulties were encountered in acquiring a site from the provincial government. The provincial government was not able to sell the C.B.C. the site and after a long period the C.B.C. was able to make arrangements for leasing a site to its satisfaction.
My point is this. The people concerned heard the announcement or read the announcement of the minister in the house that this station was going to be established a year ago last October, I think it was; I refer to the announcement. Then they expected something to happen. Nothing happened. Then the area became full of rumours. The defeated Conservative candidate announced that he had had a special message from the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) and that so and so were the facts. Then the elected member for the riding said a week or two later that he had another message from some other department of government. Then the defeated candidate said he had a later message and this was what was going to happen, and so on.
All that unnecessary concern and activity could be avoided if the C.B.C., under such circumstances, would simply issue a press release-so that people would know-that the station was going to be established, that certain difficulties had been encountered, and so on. By this means the people themselves who are going to be the patrons of this service, would understand what was happening and all these rumours and so on would be avoided.
The same thing has happened with respect to the establishment of a satellite television station in Nelson. Arrangements were being made for that station and rumours are going around that it will serve the people on this side of the mountain and not the people on the other side of the mountain, that it will serve the people on this side of the valley and not the people on the other side of the valley. Under the circumstances I think the C.B.C., as a result of study of the question by its engineers, could very well make an announcement and say they intend to locate the station at such and such a place, that it will service all the people within such and such an area, and so on.
I say that, Mr. Speaker, because I think that the senior officials of the C.B.C. on occasion take a somewhat Olympian attitude and ignore the interests of local people in the developments in television and in radio. I suggest that some system be adopted of giving accurate information-and the C.B.C. is not under security in that respect-as to the C.B.C.'s intention and so on in any particular district or area.

I had intended to have a bit to say on policy and so on but as I realize the wish of the minister to rise and reply to the many questions that have been raised, I am content at this time merely to deal with matters that are of concern to my own constituency and to others who live in the hinterlands of Canada.

It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to delay the house for very long. I am very sorry if any look on my face disturbed the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). I should much prefer to have him go on. He said he had some questions to raise with respect to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It would be interesting to hear one question raised in this house this afternoon with which one could deal instead of the grapeshot and the variety of camouflage and innuendo with which we have had to deal during the afternoon, with nothing specific whatsoever.
This is a motion to set up a committee to consider broadcasting. The motion is made pursuant to an undertaking which was given last year when the committee rose and it also was set forth in the speech from the throne.
When the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet (Mr. Fortin) spoke a short time ago I think he dealt with this matter more effectively than did anyone else when he said it was not up to one or two members of the House of Commons to decide whether the committee should be set up or whether it should not be set up but that it should be through the house itself and that, as far as he was concerned, as well as many others, this undertaking had been given and of course the committee should be set up.
I have been rather intrigued by this discussion about the great delay which has taken place in the setting up of this committee and the enormity of the offence which has been committed by this government. I have here in my hand a list of the dates of the opening and closing of parliament in years gone by in the days when a similar committee was set up; and in those days only three or four committees were set up rather than the seven, eight or nine which we have today. For instance, in the session of 1952-53 I find that the house opened on November 20, 1952. This committee or a similar committee was

set up on March 21, 1953, which is about four months after the house opened. Parliament prorogued on May 14. Hence there was there a matter of sitting time that this house would equal somewhere about the end of July. There is at least a comparable period there as at this time.
In the session of 1950 parliament opened in February. The motion was passed on April 19, two months after the house opened and parliament prorogued on June 30. One could go on and on in setting forth the facts that there never was, when hon. gentlemen opposite were sitting on the treasury benches, despite the urging of the opposition, any great disposition on their part to accelerate the business of the house despite the fact that, as I said, there were only three or four committees at the most that ever sat in those days. We never had any action such as has been deplored this afternoon because we waited from January to June to set up this committee. Who have been crying, lamenting, weeping and howling about the load that has been placed upon them by the setting up of so many committees, deploring the fact that committees are set up, asking that this cross may pass them by, that they should not have such a burden placed upon them? That is why, Mr. Speaker, I say frankly that we have deliberately delayed the setting up of this committee, important as it is.

I hear "oh, oh" from the other side. But this is the situation as of today. I have this information from the clerk of the committees. The committee on estimates is concluding its work. The committee on external affairs may have one more meeting. The committee on privileges and elections is concluding its work. The committee on railways, airlines and shipping is concluding its work or has concluded it. The committee on veterans affairs may have one more sitting. I personally feel that the committee on broadcasting is more important than is any one of those committees. However, I am only one member of this House of Commons. I am only one minister who indirectly has some responsibility for this broadcasting corporation and the board of broadcast governors whereas other ministers have a direct responsibility for their departments.
Who am I to say that broadcasting shall come first and veterans affairs shall come last? I do not propose to arrogate to myself that authority. What I propose to do is to co-operate with the House of Commons and particularly with hon. members of the opposition in order to try to arrange the business of this house so that they will not be suffering nervous breakdowns, strokes of 79951-0-3291
Broadcasting
apoplexy, and all that sort of thing, which they said would be their fate when the house opened, yet now when we are accommodating we are told we are doing something which violates the rules of the house.
I wish Lewis Carroll were here today to write Alice in Wonderland again. I think he would say something like this:
You are old, Jack the Sailor, the young man said,
And your hair has become very white;
Yet you incessantly stand on your head,
And you think at your age it is right.
I must say that I am highly flattered at being a minister, although I have no responsibility for these organizations whatsoever except in reporting to parliament. I am also highly flattered by the debate this afternoon, which has been relatively brief, a couple of hours, in that there has been no criticism of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation whatsoever. The whole time has been spent on the fact that we are bringing this motion in too late; and there have been some innuendoes about the board of broadcast governors. If the government had been inclined to accept the suggestion-which it was not because, as I said, an undertaking was given-that we should wait until another session before we set up such a committee, does anyone think that any government which adopted that course and which had any respect for the organizations and boards which it had created, in view of the innuendoes and the snide and sneering attacks which have been made on the board of broadcast governors this afternoon because of the decision in Toronto and the decision in Edmonton, would sit down and accept such snide references and agree to defer this matter?
If there is anything to be criticized with regard to decisions of the board of broadcast governors that is all the more reason why a committee should be set up this year and not next year. The fact that hon. members say in one breath that something is wrong, but in another breath say that this is not the time to bring it forward is in my opinion the best argument to suggest that there is no criticism which can be levelled at the board whatsoever.
This board was set up by this government, that is true; but I doubt if anyone in Canada can point a finger at the board of broadcast governors in any respect at all. They may disapprove of its decisions and question its decisions, but so far as suggesting that any member of the board is under the influence of the government, if that is the case we want the board in question brought before a committee of parliament and we want that board to make its defence, if such

Broadcasting
defence is necessary. In particular we want the people who are prepared to make these charges to stand up and make them and not hide behind the excuses such as we have heard this afternoon, and would we please defer this matter to next year despite the fact that the board has done a terrible thing. We do not accept that position; that is why I could not accept this afternoon the suggestion that the committee should be deferred until next year.
Mr. Speaker, as I have said there is not much to reply to in connection with this debate other than that one matter. The whole argument for the most part has been that the committee should be deferred until next year, and I think I have explained why we cannot do that. I think it is highly desirable that this committee be set up. The committee of course, not the government, Will determine its own procedure, but I hope that the first party to be brought before it will be the board of broadcast governors. The board of broadcast governors are today sitting in Halifax and are returning to sit in Ottawa during the latter part of the week. I am hopeful that if a committee is set up immediately or during this week they will have finished their sittings by the end of this week or the very first of next week, and personally I hope that the board of broadcast governors will come before this committee and give an accounting of their operations, the principles and procedures under which they function. If they are subject to criticism, then let us have that criticism aired where it can be aired effectively, definitively and properly rather than by insinuation and innuendo, as was the case this afternoon.
Second, I would hope that the C.A.B., the private broadcasters, will appear before that committee and have their opinions expressed and their judgments laid before the committee with respect to the board of broadcast governors. The most intriguing thing I know about the C.B.C. is that those who have it, if you listen to some of them, do not want it, while those who have not got it, want it. It is a very interesting problem to try to maintain this balance between those who criticize continually and those who complain because they have not got a service at all.
These are matters which can be determined by the committee when it sits rather than by my discussing them here. I do wish, however, to mention one specific matter to which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate referred when he said the budget of the C.B.C. was controlled too tightly by this government. As usual, there was some innuendo, some snide remarks, about the control which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) exercised. No minister of finance who is worth his salt -and our Minister of Finance is certainly one of the outstanding ministers of finance of Canada-can fail in his task of exercising some control over the expenditures of all the crown corporations. I want to point this out-. I have said it before, and I say it again-that when we came to power this government, whieh was going to wreck the C.B.C., this government about which so many fears were expressed and so many lamentations uttered compared to which those of Job were a paean of thanksgiving, found, when we considered the former act under which hon. gentlemen opposite had operated-and I am not criticizing them for it-these are the facts-that every expenditure over $25,000 laid out by the
Broadcasting
C.B.C. had to receive government approval. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate corrected me this afternoon-and he was probably right-saying this concerned only capital expenditure. In any event, it had to be approved by the governor in council; in other words, it had to be approved by my predecessor recommending it to the government. We raised that figure from $25,000 to $100,000 so that now the C.B.C. is free to spend any money it sees fit up to $100,000 without referring the matter to the government in any shape or form.
Is it not true that under the legislation the minister put through the house the C.B.C. had to submit a capital budget and, therefore, would such expenditures not be included in that budget?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
We are not here discussing the details of treasury board. It is perfectly true that the C.B.C. has to submit a capital budget, but the capital budget certainly does not go into details of that kind. The capital budget asks for X millions of dollars for capital development, and that is all there is in it.
This is an important step, as I have tried to indicate, and I think it is a point in which the people of Canada are particularly interested. They are concerned about any government or political party exercising influence over the programming of a great national organization. Not only did we change the act so as to raise the floor from $25,000 to $100,000, but we said at the same time that there should be no control of expenditures whatsoever so far as programming is concerned. I know of programs upon which the C.B.C. is embarked-whether they are good or not is not for me to say, but I am thinking of programs such as the R.C.M. Police series-whose costs are running today into hundreds of thousands of dollars over the whole period. These costs have been approved by the C.B.C. without any reference to the. government whatsoever. So when the hon. gentleman attacks us about cost, as he says prostituting broadcasting or too tight budgeting control, I do think, with all due respect to a man whom I respect and like personally, that he was talking sheer nonsense, and no one knows this better than the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
I dissent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I shall not say very much more this afternoon. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) spent some time dealing with the board of broadcast governors. Broadcasting
Canada, in the delightful condition in which the country finds itself today it is rather hard to find intelligent men and women to appoint to a board who do not, like the majority of intelligent men and women in this country, support the present administration. Surely, with all due respect to the members of the C.C.F., we are at liberty to choose those whom we think best fitted to occupy such positions as these rather than from the somewhat dilapidated remains of the once great party represented opposite.
We have chosen men and women who are, very largely, independent, and it is surely strange for anyone in the C.C.F. party to be questioning the judgment of a board of which Dr. Eugene Forsey is one of the leading members. I never expected to see that day, with respect to the C.C.F. One could go on and list Dr. Emlyn Davies, and many others; people who, because of their intelligence, I hope support the government, though in fact no one has any knowledge of whether they do or not. Indeed, we could not care less because they are men and women of integrity whose judgment the country respects and we are prepared to accept their decisions. That is the situation with respect to this board.
The hon. member for Laurier also made some passing reference to a statement made by the premier of Quebec about proposed interference with the C.B.C. I fail to see where that statement has shown any interference, but I am not going to get involved in the internal politics of Quebec. In response to the question by Senator Croll as to whether that was in July he said "around there". Q. When did you visit my office?

As you can see, Mr. Chairman, there is a conflict here with respect to whose recommendation he acted on when he went to see his wife. Would the hon. member permit a question? By referring to these conflicts in the evidence is he imputing collusion between the two parties or would he agree that it is sensible and probably good law that if evidence exists as in this case that the respondent is living with another man there is absolutely nothing wrong in the husband going to see his wife and discussing the matter? Because we have been prevented by the rules, and probably quite properly so, from discussing what constitutes collusion, I do not think I can be accused of imputing collusion here. I did make use of the word because, as I have said, it is my general understanding that it means that two people work together and attempt to present evidence to the body which will be granting the divorce. I do not know whether it is permissible in law for a husband and wife to agree that each will appear and give evidence about one of them having committed adultery. I do not know whether it puts a different light on the matter if they both agree that one of them will be caught in compromising circumstances by investigators in order to provide evidence to support a charge of adultery.
As I say, we have been prevented from going into the question of what is and what is not collusion. I hope that answers my friend's question with respect to whether I am imputing collusion to these two parties. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I must advise the hon. member that his time has expired.

This is one of some 450 cases that are before us for determination at this particular session of parliament. As in most cases, this petition is from a person who lives in the province of Quebec and who comes from a somewhat humble rung of society in that particular province. In short, this man comes before us, as have a good many others, because his means are limited and parliament is the only way that he can obtain relief from a marriage which, to all practical intents and purposes, has long since been dissolved.
The petitioner in this particular case is 40 years old. He lives in the city of Montreal and he is a private chauffeur. He was married on June 4, 1947 and 13 years later he
Private Bills-Divorce
is before parliament asking that his marriage be dissolved because his wife is no longer living with him and indeed, as is clearly established by the evidence to the satisfaction of any reasonable person, his wife has been committing adultery, if you want to put it in that way, or living as man and wife, if you want to put it in that way, for four or five years with another man.
There have been suggestions made, and they are the type of suggestions we hear so often-these little legal phrases that make my blood boil when they come from the depths and wells of ignorance-I refer to phrases about collusion and so on, putting a tarnish on a very proper case and then just left there so that we in parliament who have this duty are somehow tarnished ourselves because we are trying to help decide the merits of a petition.
As far as any inference of collusion is concerned in this case, I say that there is not one jot or tittle of evidence to suggest that anything like that took place. Here we have the woman leaving her home for four or five years. She has lived with somebody else as man and wife. Any conversation that her husband has had with her to help him procure evidence to present to the committee of the other place and by the reports being presented before us is clearly not collusion. I repeat again that for reasonable minds and reasonable men this person, 40 years old, a humble person, from the province of Quebec, is coming before us asking for justice and the proper dissolution of the marriage that, to all intents and purposes disappeared four or five years ago. The challenge I put to the two hon. members opposite who have been carrying out this scandalous-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

The challenge I put to the hon. members opposite is that they must decide within a few minutes whether they are going to grant this man his just rights or whether they are going to deny him those rights.
The hon. member need not challenge me to anything. From what I have indicated so far, it is quite evident what our position is.
What is your position on the bill before us?

If the hon. member had followed the trend of the discussion perhaps he would have discovered that position already. Let me say once more, Mr. Chairman, that my argument here is with respect to the point in the petition, and this is what I think perhaps is being glossed over. The petition

states "and more particularly that on or about July 10, 1959" in the city of Montreal and so on adultery was committed. It makes reference to this particular date. There is evidence here as I indicated. The corespondent appeared. He is asked questions by Mr. Cohen. He is asked whether he had been living together with the respondent as man and wife:
-"and more particularly, were you on the 10th day of July" and he says "yes". Then he is asked "Have you committed adultery with-?" and he gives the name of the respondent there, and the answer is yes. However, he does not answer that they committed adultery one with the other or that he committed adultery with her or however it took place on that particular date. That is the point I should like to make. We have mentioned this point on a number of occasions in connection with cases where there is evidence of a common law arrangement between a couple.
It is not common law.
My hon. friend can squirm around in his seat and say that there is an argument, if he so wishes, as to whether it is or is not common law.
It is not common law.

That is the general term that laymen understand or that I understand. It may not be the term that my hon. and learned friend understands and wants to apply to these things, under a strict application. I assume that the proper term or phraseology would just be that they were living together as man and wife. I do not know whether that is the proper term to apply to situations such as this one. However, that is the term used in evidence given before the committee of the other place. I have seen both of them, namely reference to a common law arrangement and reference to a couple living together as man and wife. If it would suit the sensitivities of my friend the hon. member for Halifax I shall be glad to comply and make reference to his living together as man and wife.
I say that, in my opinion, evidence to that effect is sufficient grounds to grant a divorce. But to attempt to ask this committee-and this is what they are doing-to put in a petition that adultery took place on a particular day and then give no evidence at all that it took place on that particular day is stretching the point quite a bit, in my opinion.
I am not prepared to vote in favour of the passing of this particular bill on the ground that adultery was committed on the tenth day of July, 1959, because nowhere in evidence
tMr. Howard.]

is it stated that adultery was committed on that particular date. I am prepared to vote in favour of this bill on the ground that the respondent and the corespondent have been living together as I put it, common law, or, as my sensitive friend the hon. member for Halifax wants it put, have been living together as man and wife. That is the ground upon which I am prepared to vote in support of this particular bill. The discussion I was leading up to was to point out that, regardless of the conflict in the evidence of the petitioner and further on between the respondent and the corespondent, which may be inconsequential things, on the basis of this couple-

I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but apparently he insists on this particular date. Did he overlook the third line in paragraph 7 of the petition where it is alleged "that on or about July 10, 1959", not necessarily on that particular date.
Quite right.
Did the hon. member notice that?
Yes. I read that phraseology previously, namely "on or about".
What do you say?

I do not know what the word "about" means to start with. There is no evidence that adultery took place on July 10 or about July 10. Does this mean within six months, two months, a week, or what? There is no attempt to specify it. The only reference here is an admission by the petitioner that his wife told him she had committed adultery at some time in the past, and an admission by the respondent that she was living as man and wife with another individual named. The word "adultery" is not even used in the questions submitted to her or the answers she gave. There is only the reference to her living with someone else as man and wife, particularly on the evening of July 10, 1959.

I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question, or it is a point of information. Under normal court procedure you could not ask a leading question using the word adultery, such as the question "Did you commit adultery?", giving a particular night, because that is the point in issue. A court would not allow that form of questioning on that ground.

I did not know that. If that is the case, apparently the committee in the other place does not follow that practice because Mr. Cohen is allowed to ask such a leading question of the corespondent. It is not only a leading question in the sense of

"Have you committed adultery?", but he puts it quite emphatically almost forcing the witness to say yes. He asks: "And you have committed adultery with the corespondent?", and the answer is yes.
That would not be allowed either.

While this form of questioning may not be acceptable in a court of law, apparently it is acceptable in the committee of the other place because even though Mr. Cohen does not pose that question to the respondent, he is allowed to pose it in a very direct way to the corespondent. Therefore, I think perhaps the rules in a court of law are probably not followed in the committee of the other house, and members of the other place consider themselves, as perhaps we do, not as a court of law but as legislators passing a law and in reality the grounds can be as broad or as narrow as we so choose.
Would the hon. member permit a further question. Is he prepared to vote now in favour of this petition?

I am not going to vote for the petition at all, because I do not think the petition is before us. What is before us is a bill, and as you have pointed out on a number of occasions, Mr. Chairman, we are at the moment on clause 1 which says that the marriage is hereby dissolved, et cetera. This is the point I indicated I would vote for and I wish to indicate on what grounds I will vote for it. It is not that adultery has been proven to be committed on July 10 or about, but that adultery at some time has been committed on the evidence of the corespondent. speechtext: House in committee of the whole on a certain proposed resolution to amend the Judges Act. Shall the resolution carry?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think I should, for the benefit of the committee, make a brief explanation of the main purposes and provisions of the legislation to be based on the resolution now before the committee. This resolution and the bill which will be introduced when it carries are in large measure complementary
Judges Act
to the resolution which was recently before the house to provide for an address to Her Majesty asking that she will cause to be laid before the United Kingdom parliament a measure to amend the British North America Act to provide for a retirement age of 75 for all judges of superior courts in Canada. In the view of the government the two measures should be considered as interdependent and the passage of this one is in a very real sense, or should be in a very real sense, dependent upon the passage of the other resolution through this parliament.
The reason why we hold this view is that the occasion of the introduction of this resolution and the main purpose of the legislation are to adjust the pensions of judges who will be now, all of them in Canada, retiring at the age of 75 years. We consider, therefore, that at a time when we are completing the program which will bring about the retirement of all judges at the age of 75 it is especially desirable to put the pensions of judges appointed by parliament on a proper footing. It is my own submission, Mr. Chairman, that for a number of years our judges have not had proper provision with respect to the annuities which they receive on their retirement or which their wives and widows receive on their decease.
Although, as I have said, we regard the main occasion or reason for this measure as being the simultaneous presentation to parliament of the measure regarding retirement age, there are other reasons for its introduction which I suggest may be best understood by a reference to the main provisions of the measure which will follow this resolution.
I should say a word about the desirability of providing adequately for the judiciary of our country. There are, of course, a number of fields in which this problem confronts us, but the main field in which I propose to deal with it tonight is in that of their retirement allowances. Of course this field is closely related to the field of salaries; but the measure, I should like to make clear, does not touch the salaries of judges. It deals with their retirement allowances, the provisions for their retirement, and also with the provision for travelling allowances while they are on circuit or travelling on judicial duty.
I think it is a fact-a principle, if you like-which will not be disputed by hon. members of this house, that not only is it essential that we should make provision for the adequate compensation of our judiciary while they hold office but, as an essential part of the position of the judiciary generally, adequate provision should be made for their situation after they will have retired from

Judges Act
office, because it is a fact that in the vast majority of cases those who accepted appointments to the bench have in the past, and I am sure they will in the future, accepted those appointments at a very real sacrifice in terms of the immediate monetary compensation which they receive.
This, of course, is in itself not an improper feature because there is attached to the position of the judiciary the attributes which surround one of the highest, if not the highest, positions in the land. There is an element of public service. There is, of course, also the position and the esteem in which our judges are properly held. All of these things are attributes of judicial office, and they are essential attributes of judicial office; but I think that one must always also take a realistic and practical approach to this matter and not allow one's regard for the attraction which individuals so appointed might properly feel to this high position to outweigh the fact that it is not right that we should ask them to make too great a sacrifice, a completely disproportionate sacrifice, when we call upon them to assume that office.
One of the features with regard to this office and to the position of judges is this question of the retirement allowances which they will receive when they retire. As I said a moment ago, the reasons for the introduction of this particular measure may be understood by reference to its main provisions, the principle one of those being the revision of the rules and regulations regarding retirement allowances for judges,
The main change we are making in this connection is to adjust what I believe to have been an unfortunate provision introduced in the amendment to the Judges Act of 1955. As a result of that amendment judges retirement allowances have been based upon the salaries that they were receiving prior to 1955. By the amendment of 1955 an increase with respect to superior court judges of $2,500 in their salaries was provided for; but it was a part of that amendment that their pensions, their retirement allowances, should have relation not to the new salary but to the salary that had been in effect before that change of 1955. The result has been that up to the present time our judges have been retiring on a pension based on the salaries which were set in 1951.
For the information of hon. members it should be recalled that judges retire on two thirds of the salary which is set as the basis of their pension. So that the situation now is that all judges in Canada retire on two thirds of their 1951 salary and it has been felt by the government that it was and is a mistake to relate the retiring allowances

of judges to their former salaries. Most, if not all, of the persons for whom parliament makes provision with respect to pension or superannuation have that pension provision related to the salary of which they were in receipt at the time of their retirement. This, of course, was always the situation with respect to the Judges Act until the amendment of 1955, but the result of that amendment has been to relate the retirement allowances of our judiciary not to the actual salary received at the time of their retirement but to the salary they received some years prior to the last amendment.
One of the other effects of this situation has been not only general in its nature with respect to the question of whether or not it is a sound principle but it has also had the result that again of those for whom parliament provides retirement allowances under federal legislation judges alone have had no revision of their retirement allowances since the year 1951. As I have explained, in the revision of 1955 it was provided that judges would retire on a pension based on their previous salary, which has had the effect that their pension rates have not been changed since the year 1951. So far as I have been able to ascertain they are the only group for whom we are responsible who have waited this long for an adjustment in the level of their retirement allowances.
I think I should also emphasize to the committee that the changes to be proposed in the legislation itself will also affect the wives and widows of those judges who are covered by the provisions we make for their annuities. It is the intention that all those who have retired since 1955 will also have their situations and those of their wives and widows covered by the provisions that will be introduced in the bill to follow the resolution.

speechtext: Since 1955 or 1951?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Since 1955. Another main group of provisions in the legislation will be those affecting the circumstances under which judges may receive retirement allowances on their retirement. It will be provided that in the future for any judge to be entitled to a full retirement allowance when he reaches the retirement age of 75 he must have served 10 years on the bench. When I say "in the future" I mean with respect to any future appointments. The implications of this will be obvious. It is our feeling that when we are asking parliament to provide for a retirement age of 75 we should at the same time suggest and lay before parliament this proposal that a judge will hot have earned his full retirement allowance for his judicial

functions unless he has served 10 years in that capacity. This, of course, must be read subject to the provisions for retirement on account of sickness or on account of other considerations in the national interest, but in general a judge appointed in the future who is in good health and reaches the retirement age of 75 must have served 10 years before he will be qualified for a full retirement allowance.
"We are also proposing to change the provision with regard to the receipt of annuities on voluntary retirement, At the present time a judge may only receive the full annuity to which he is entitled if he retires on account of sickness and it is found that that retirement is in the public interest. We propose to make three changes in this situation. We propose to provide that any judge who has served 15 years in judicial office may retire on full annuity at the age of 70. This retirement will be entirely voluntary but it is our feeling that there are cases, and an appreciable number of them, in which the interests of the judiciary as well as the position of the individual judge may well warrant retirement of that judge at the age of 70. It is our feeling, therefore, that if after having served for 15 years in a judicial capacity any individual judge feels that he should retire he may do so at the age of 70 and receive the full retirement allowance. It will be realized, of course, that the provision of 15 years service is closely related to the present 15-year provision with regard to certain of the existing retirement arrangements.
The second change to be made in this field is that if at any time after having served 15 years a judge wishes to retire and if, in the opinion of the governor in council, his retirement will contribute to the better administration of justice or is in the national interest, that judge may also be permitted to retire voluntarily and receive the full retirement allowance. The third provision to be made in the new legislation with respect to voluntary retirement is that if by reason of sickness or other disability a judge is rendered unable to discharge the full functions of his office then again he may be permitted to retire with a full retirement allowance.
I am quite sure the committee will realize without my going into detail that there have been a number of occasions in the past when the present provision with regard to retirement, related strictly as it is to the question of sickness and the public interest, have created very great difficulties not only for the present government but also, I know, for the former government with respect to whether in fact retirement should be accepted and the pension or retirement allowance should be
Judges Act
paid. What we are seeking to do, therefore, is to clarify and bring more into accord with the actual position the provisions with regard to the circumstances under which judges may be allowed to retire on full pension before they reach the age of 75.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Does the 15 years apply to the third case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
No, the 15 years does not apply to the case of sickness or other incapacity disabling a judge from the due fulfillment of his judicial office.
The third main provision that is being made in the legislation is with respect to living allowances. At the present time there is in my view a rather artificial distinction between the amounts that judges may receive for living allowances or expenses when they proceed on circuit or go on journeys in connection with their judicial functions. There is an artificial distinction between communities with a population of 5,000 or less and those with a population of 5,000 or over. Generally it is provided that if a judge attends as a judge at a centre of 5,000 population or less he is entitled to living expenses of $8 a day. If the centre is over 5,000 the amount is $12 a day. There is provision that in special circumstances these rates may be increased from $8 to $12 and from $12 to $15 a day respectively. It does not, I am sure, take much argument to convince the committee that there are very few, if any, communities in Canada today where a judge can live for $15, let alone $12 or $8, a day. Yet, these are the full amounts that he may be allowed for living expenses while in that community away from his home.
There have been cases where I know judges have economized in ways that I am sure this committee would readily agree no member of the judiciary should be expected to adopt. They have to economize because, contrary to popular belief, judges are not all rich people before they are appointed and they are certainly not all rich people on the basis of the salaries we pay them. Judges do find a very real drain upon their income when they travel, as they do sometimes, on lengthy journeys on circuit. I should like anyone to reflect for a moment and ask himself the question whether a judge coming from Toronto to Ottawa to take the assizes can possibly live and pay his hotel expenses on $15 a day, although that is the maximum that judges are authorized to receive. Some of them, therefore, do economize, to use a polite term, with regard to the places where they stay. This is not a proper position, nor I believe is it a fair position, in which to put members of the judiciary.

Judges Act
We propose to make, not an extravagant change but what I regard as a very practical change in that situation by simply providing that a judge who is absent from his home on judicial duties will be entitled to living allowance in accord with the expenses that he has actually incurred. All a judge will have to do will be to file a statement of his actual living expenses while away from home on judicial duties and he will be entitled to recover that amount. This, it seems to me, is not what can be described as a really generous gesture with respect to our judges. It only means they will be entitled to recover what they have actually paid out while absent from their homes in the service of their country.
There will be one or two other minor changes with respect to travel and living allowances, principally a change that will place the province of Quebec once more on the same footing as all other provinces. This change will have the result that judges in Quebec will no longer have to have their travel and living expenses certified by the chief judge of their court. In no other province is that required, and it seems to us it is anomalous in the extreme that judges in Quebec should be subject to that requirement when no others are.
These, Mr. Chairman, are the main provisions of the legislation which will be based on this resolution. They are, I believe, a first very practical step in the direction of revising the situation of the judiciary. They are a concurrent step with the one which parliament was asked to ratify regarding retirement ages. We will, in the future, when this legislation carries, be in a position where all judges appointed by this parliament retire at 75 years of age and where the conditions and circumstances under which they receive their retirement allowances and the amount of those retirement allowances will have been placed on a rational basis, in my view. The other circumstances with regard to the performance of their functions, that is those relating to their allowances while travelling, also will have been rationalized and placed on the same acceptable basis.
There are I recognize, and I am sure the committee will agree, a number of other features of the Judges Act which call for study and review. Those are still under study and review. I am not able to say when I shall be introducing legislation to deal with them, but I believe that with the measure which I am placing before parliament tonight we are making a useful first step forward in connection with the physical and financial position of our judiciary.

Judges Act
there was any violation of the independence of the judiciary in the minds of those who expressed concern on that point and also whether there was, with regard to judges now on the bench, any breach of contract or any breach of implied contract.
With regard to the judges who are now on the bench and who, after the parliament of the United Kingdom will have dealt with the matter, will be forced to retire, one wonders whether or not the minister has met the argument-admittedly it was not accepted on the other side but it is one that was made with sincerity and conviction in this house a few days ago-that to cause a judge to retire under circumstances of which he could not be expected to be aware at the time of appointment, was a matter that involved a breach of ^/hat I would call at least an implied contract. I am aware of the fact that the other night we used the phrase "breach of contract". Possibly that was too loose a use of the expression "breach of contract". There was not a contract in the sense perhaps of an enforceable contract at law but there were certainly present all of the elements of what one might regard as an arrangement between the state and the judicial appointee having all the qualities of a contractual arrangement which the state would feel at least morally bound to recognize as imposing on it an obligation not less than the kind of obligation that would have been imposed if an arrangement of some sort based on the same principle had prevailed between individuals, one of whom was not a judge and the other who did not represent the crown.
I suggest to the Minister of Justice that the argument of "breach of contract" in the sense in which I have mentioned it tonight is a sound one and is one that is not met by this resolution. Those judges who are now on the bench and who in the future will be forced to retire will retire under circumstances that were not present, were not made known to them or could not have been presumed at the time of appointments. I have no hesitation in saying that the government is justified-and the house is with the government-in suggesting that judges should retire at the age of 75. That is not a matter in issue. What is in issue in so far as I am concerned is that this failure to provide for an economic treatment of judges now on the bench, in a manner that would not in any way put them in a less advantageous position than they would be in if there was no compulsory period of retirement, is an act which in principle-and if you will, only theoretically at this stage-involves a breach of contract and, I submit, moreover

is a violation in principle again of the independence which all of us in this house want to see the judiciary have in Canada. That principle was argued in this house in 1927, in 1930, in 1933 and in 1954 was thoroughly discussed in the parliament of the United Kingdom. There the position was taken, as I reminded the house the other night, by Mr. Churchill among others, that any economic treatment of the judges that would be less than what they would be entitled to pursuant to the terms of their appointment would be regarded and must be regarded as a violation of the kind of independence which in that island they regard the judges as being deserving of, which indeed they regard as one of the essential conditions of guaranteeing the integrity and independence of the bench.
However, in the resolution and the bill based on it which the minister will introduce the government does not accept this argument because the judges who are now on the bench will retire on the same annuity terms as judges who have yet to be appointed. I contend that that is wrong on the two grounds I have mentioned. It is wrong on the ground that it is a violation of the terms of the arrangement, and for me more particularly it is a violation of the kind of independence which I believe our judiciary should possess.
That is not an empty statement. Whether the argument which has provoked it is accepted or not, we will all agree, I think, on the necessity of recognizing how important in a free society the judicial arm is. We pride ourselves on the preservation of freedom in this country, and rightly so. We know that one of the reasons for the preservation or existence of that freedom is because, unlike in totalitarian countries, our judiciary is not, and is not under any circumstances encouraged to be influenced in any way by the executive or by political or any other considerations than those which should attend an absolute regard for judicial objectivity.
So I feel that we are making a mistake in principle in treating judges on the bench now who will have to retire at the age of 75 in the way that they will be treated under this particular measure. No great economic loss or inconvenience would result if we had made, or were even now to make, a differentiation between judges on the bench and the financial terms of their retirement as distinguished from the situation in that regard which under this measure we are going to apply to judges yet to be appointed and the circumstances of their retirement. However, the government has given this matter its consideration; it has taken this

position and I can do no more than point out what I believe to be the unsound position it takes.
I agree with the minister that our judges should be able to retire in dignity. In saying that I am not oblivious of the fact that in dealing with the judges consideration must be given at some other time to the retirement circumstances of other classes of people in our community. I am not going to say, as one could easily be tempted to say, that the pension requirements of other classes in the community deserve attention. That I assume we will all recognize to be the case. We are now dealing with the judges. The judiciary is an important institution in our country and it must be surrounded by the kind of economic security which will enable it to discharge its functions ably, objectively and honourably; and I say that without in any way being open to the suggestion that I am oblivious of the need to provide satisfactory retirement schemes for the people of Canada as well as for other groups in our country.
The minister said that the annuities for the widows of judges are not adequate at the present time and that he proposes to take steps to deal with this problem. When the bill is presented to the house we shall be able to examine that question. He pointed out that judges now retire on salaries fixed in 1951. That being the situation I think we will have to recognize the equity of the matter and raise the level of annuities in relation not to the salary of nine years ago but to the salary of the present day.
As the minister has said, and I think we would all agree he has said rightly, the annuity paid to a judge should not be related to a former salary but should be based upon the salary which under the law is given at the time of retirement. Certainly this matter is one that should now come before the house, because as the minister has said there has been no revision since 1951.
The minister then spoke of judges retiring on a voluntary basis, and in that connection he said that there were three changes in contemplation. In the first case a full annuity would be provided to a judge at the age of 70 providing that judge had been on the bench for 15 years. The second case had to do with judges retiring after 15 years, if in the national interest he should do so. I will be interested when the bill is presented in knowing precisely what the minister means by "in the national interest". Incidentally, in all three of these cases, the judge will receive, I understand, the full annuity. As I say, I will be interested to know what the term "in the national interest" means in this particular
Judges Act
situation. Does voluntary retirement mean that a judge is retiring because of criticism of his administration, because of criticism of his capacity or because of a possible intervention that might be made to have him removed? Would that warrant a consideration of the matter "in the national interest"? In any event, Mr. Chairman, when the bill is presented I would want to know more about what is meant in that regard.
Then the minister instanced the third case where retirement of a judge is voluntary because of sickness or disability. The full annuity is provided in that case, and as the minister pointed out in answer to a question of mine, voluntary retirement can take place even though a judge may have been on the bench for less than 15 years.
The minister then dealt with the matter of travelling allowances, and I think this general statement by him will appeal to all of us, knowing the cost of living particularly in the larger communities of our country. As I understood the scale, it will be from $8 to $12 and then to $15 a day, beginning at $12 where the judge was presiding in a community of over 5,000 people. I did not catch what the circumstances were with regard to the amount of $15, but I suspect that would depend upon the cost of living in a community likewise over 5,000 people.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I thank the minister; I did not catch that. It is based on actual living expenses, and I thank him for correcting me on that point. While I am dealing with this, I will simply observe in passing that this principle might possibly be applied to other public servants, notably those serving Canada at the United Nations. I am not referring to members of parliament or members of the government but to the public servants who work in New York and whose per diem allowance is not, as I recollect it, altogether adequate.
The minister pointed out that hereafter judges in the province of Quebec will have their travelling allowances approved on the same basis as judges in the other nine provinces. I do not know why in the past a different arrangement was made, and it may be that when the bill is before us in committee we shall have an opportunity of going into this matter further.
Finally, the minister said there would be other matters which would ultimately be dealt

Judges Act
with by way of legislation. He indicated there were other questions he had under review. He did not, however, say what those matters were, and it might be possible for the hon. gentleman when he concludes this debate, to give us some information in that regard.
Briefly, to summarize what I have said, I repeat that in principle this resolution is one that is acceptable to those of us in the official opposition. We shall want some explanation along the lines I have mentioned with regard to the federal government's acceptance of only four federal judges in the province of Quebec when seven were asked for. That can only mean that the government will have to indicate why the seven asked for by the province of Quebec were not warranted in the circumstances. No doubt the minister will give us his point of view in that regard.
Then there is the argument that I made, and which I believe to be a sound one, that we are here concerned with the independence of the judiciary and the decision to treat judges now on the bench on terms similar to those to be appointed from this date onward. This is a matter which we regard as a vital one, affecting not any individual judge but the whole of the judiciary which in a free society is no less important in the preserving of good order in the state than are the other arms of government.
Our system of government could not possibly function if alongside the executive and parliament we did not have an objective, neutral, capable and industrious judiciary not open to interference or influence from any quarter. I am not suggesting that our judiciary is open to such influence, but because we want to take the greatest possible care to ensure that it is not, I again tell the minister and the house that we shall examine with interest the bill on which this resolution is based.
Finally, I say again that no one can say from anything we have said on this side of the house in support of this measure that there is a failure to appreciate that the problem of the retirement of other classes in our community is still a problem that has to be dealt with. We are not seeking to deal with those matters tonight, but we ought to be able to deal with all these matters on terms that do not necessarily affect objective consideration of the case of each group.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not for a moment suggest that I have the same knowledge and understanding of this subject as has the distinguished member for Essex East who has just resumed his seat, an hon. gentleman who is a distinguished member of the

bar and who has demonstrated on occasion after occasion his great capacity to plead lost causes in this house.
However, speaking for this group, I must say that judging from the minister's explanation the proposed amendments to the Judges Act to be based on this resolution appear to us to be reasonable and founded on humane considerations of the need of judges' status, their responsibilities to the nation, their duties and their requirements. I listened carefully while the Minister of Justice was making his explanation and while, as I said before, I have not the detailed knowledge of this subject which the hon. member for Essex East possesses I think the explanation the minister gave was very reasonable and very fair. On that account this group will be pleased to support this resolution.
However-don't clap-I must say we do hope that the government will soon give some humane consideration to the needs of disability pensioners many of whom are on war veterans allowance; to the needs of those on old age security relief and a considerable number of persons in Canada who are unemployed and not able to receive unemployment insurance benefits. Like the hon. member for Essex East, I hope the government gives early consideration-similar consideration-to the needs of these people in our society. With those few remarks I will conclude, though I may possibly have more to say on second reading.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Essex East has dealt with our position on this side of the house and I have no intention of repeating the points he put forward. I think all of us would agree with most of the points which were made by the Minister of Justice in bringing in this resolution, subject, of course, to what will be contained in the bill.
It is impossible on the resolution stage of any bill to give complete consent to what may be contained in the measure itself but I do not think we on this side can quarrel with the greater part of the statements made by the Minister of Justice. There are, however, one or two things which I should like to bring to his attention.
One of them has already been dealt with by my hon. friend from Essex East, and that is the number of judges in the province of Quebec. The minister said at the outset that this matter had slipped his mind and that he had therefore made no reference to it. I will not repeat the arguments of my hon. friend other than to put it this way; that I know there is a great shortage of superior court judges in the city of Montreal. The Minister of Justice is perhaps far more aware

than I am of the tremendous number of cases which have to be handled from day to day in the various courts of that city. With the increasing population, and for other reasons, it becomes every day more necessary and more important to have additional judges. I shall say no more as far as the request from the province of Quebec is concerned.
I presume that when the request was made and approved of by the legislative assembly it was done after careful consideration with the chief justices of the various districts in the province of Quebec. However, I notice the minister said that it was the intention to appoint four judges at this time. It may well be that the minister, after consultation with the provincial authorities and with those who are in touch with the various districts of the province of Quebec, may come to the conclusion either before the bill is brought in or at a later date that the needs of justice and of the national interest as he put it, would be met by an additional number of judges.
Then there is the point dealing with the question I raised at the end of his remarks, namely that the minister takes it that this resolution is complementary to the one which was discussed in the house recently and that the two are interdependent. I simply want to support the view of my colleague, the hon. member for Essex East, and our position taken at the time of the discussion of the earlier resolution which sought to amend the British North America Act, and the attitude taken by us at that time. We felt then and we feel now that there should be included in this bill consideration of those judges who had certainly an implied contract when they were appointed. Surely, they could not be presumed to know that at a later date an amendment such as that which was made earlier and that which is now contained in the bill which will follow this resolution would be enacted.
In so far as the other matters are concerned, I think that we on this side of the house And ourselves in agreement with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC, FOR GRANTING ANNUITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
There are one or two points which I should like to reply to before the resolution carries. I appreciate the position taken and the comments made by hon. members opposite with respect to the question of the provision which is to be made for those who are compulsorily retired, but I am sorry we will apparently not be able to reconcile our views in that regard. However, I point out that while I do not in any way retreat from my view that there is an absolute right in this parliament, in conjunction with provincial governments, to make amendments to the British North America Act in this field, I do agree, and
Judges Act
said at the time of the earlier debate that I did agree that one must take account of the financial position of those who will be affected thereby. In fairness and in decency one must do that.
I therefore point out that under this resolution the positions of those judges who will be affected by the introduction of the retirement age, will be very appreciably improved, not perhaps to the full extent that would have been done by the measure suggested by my hon. friends, namely that they retire on full salary, but their financial position will be appreciably improved and brought closer to that point. Certainly, I would suggest that in a large number of cases, particularly those appointed a number of years ago, their positions will be brought up to the level of at least the salary prevailing at the time they were appointed. I think that at least meets the argument of my hon. friends in effect even though we are not entirely agreed in principle.
The other point that I should like to reply to is the question of the extra judges for the province of Quebec. I regret very much to have to apologize to the committee for having made an error. I think I said the Quebec legislature provided six for Montreal and one for Three Rivers. I should have said five for Montreal and one for Three Rivers. The total provided by their legislation is six. We are asking parliament to authorize salaries for four.
My hon. friend will, I know, understand that I am not for a moment disagreeing with the fact of the need for additional judges in the Montreal area where five are provided for provincially. I think my hon. friends will also agree that five is a substantial number of judges to ask parliament to provide salaries for and to appoint at one fell swoop. The fact that we are asking for salaries for only three now should not be taken as an indication that we think three will meet the problem. It is only an indication-and I hope it will only be taken as an indication- that we are asking for three and intend to appoint three at the present time and that we shall have another look at the situation as soon as possible at, say, the next session.
This has been discussed with the provincial authorities and while they do not moderate their position, as one would not expect them to with respect to the need, they have agreed that the provision of three extra judges at this time, as soon as we can do it, will be a real contribution toward meeting that need. Therefore, there is no difficulty between us on this point.
With respect to the other question that was raised in this connection, that is the propriety
5230	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act of the federal authority in not filling immediately the number of positions provided for by the provinces, there are two cases that I can cite which might serve as a precedent for this. There is the case of Prince Edward Island. There has been on the statute books of that province for many years provision for an extra judge which position has not yet been filled, and there is the case of Saskatchewan where originally there were provided positions for 20 district court judges. By agreement with the province the actual number to be appointed for years was set at 18. It is only recently that Saskatchewan legislation has actually been changed to provide positions for only 16; so that for all those years, until last year, although their legislation provided for 20, Saskatchewan asked Ottawa to appoint only 18, and that was the number that we in fact appointed, notwithstanding the provision made by their legislature. Therefore, there is no new or startling precedent in the fact that for a short period although five have been authorized for Montreal by the provincial legislature we are appointing only three, I emphasize that this is merely the situation for the present. It does go, and it is agreed by the provincial authorities to go a long way toward meeting the need they felt when they asked their legislature to provide for five further positions.
These, I think, Mr. Chairman, are the two main points raised by my hon. friends opposite. As they said, when they see the bill there may be other specific questions that will come up and I shall endeavour at that time to give such further explanations as the house may wish.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

When this debate was last adjourned the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) had raised a point of order which I shall be glad to deal with very briefly now. The point of order was raised as a result of lengthy quotations by the hon.


member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) from the Winnipeg Free Press. I am sorry the hon. member is not here at the moment. The point made was that our practice does not permit the reading of such extracts in a debate, which is correct. I refer the house to Beauchesne, fourth edition, citation 157, paragraphs 5 and 7. Paragraph 5 reads as follows:
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the house and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the house.
That is the general rule and practice. Although I had some thought there might be some difference between a case where the article quoted was against the interests of the member speaking and a case where it was in favour of the point of view he was expressing I think that perhaps the better view is that such articles should not be read at all. If it is against the interests of the member speaking and amounts to a question of privilege then paragraph 7 of the same citation applies. It is in the following terms:
When a complaint is made Of a newspaper, it is the practice in the House of Commons of Canada for the member to rise on a question of privilege and point out that he has been libelled or misrepresented. He may read as much of the article as is necessary to prove his case but he cannot go farther. He is bound to confine himself strictly to the question of privilege.
In effect what the hon. member was doing was dealing with a question of privilege in the course of the debate, and in my view the point taken by the minister was well taken.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-32, to authorize the construction and maintenance of a bridge across the St. Lawrence river at or near the town of La Salle, in the province of Quebec.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I hope the temper of the house will be the same when I am finished. May I say that this is a simple bill
79951-0-330
Bridges
which is merely a formality. Its purpose is to authorize the province of Quebec to go ahead with the building of a building- excuse me, I am talking about buildings all the time because I am so overwrought on account of the housing problems-the building of a bridge adjacent to the Mercier bridge. It will be a one-way bridge to take the traffic load from the town of La Salle to the south side of the river off the Mercier bridge. The building of the bridge involves parliament in no responsibility other than the fact that because of the Navigable Waters Protection Act it becomes necessary to get the authorization of parliament for the building of any structure across navigable waters.
