speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LA SALLE, QUE.  AUTHORIZATION FOR CON- STRUCTION ACROSS ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think there will be, and in fact I am sure there will not be any objection to this legislation. None the less, there are some things I think should be said at this time on the subject of the construction of this bridge. I hope the minister will not take issue with what I am about to say. I am in agreement with him that by virtue of section 11 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, no approval shall be given under this part for the site or plan of any bridge over the St. Lawrence. In other words, because of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, no bridge can be built over the St. Lawrence except by authorization of special legislation. It cannot be done by virtue of the act, but it may be done by a separate bill such as is being done in this case. This was done in the case of the construction of the present Mercier bridge which links Caugh-nawaga with Ville La Salle, and was done in the case of the Victoria bridge as well as in the case of the Jacques Cartier bridge.
My main purpose in rising was to make some reference to the traffic conditions in the city of Montreal, that is the conditions separating the island from the south shore. I am sure that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and also the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), who has been in his post for perhaps a lesser period of time than the Minister of Transport, are well aware of the very difficult transportation problem that exists in Montreal. They are brought about by a number of reasons. They are brought about by an increase in the population of greater Montreal. They are brought about by economic conditions. They are brought about by a tremendous development on the south

Bridges
shore that includes the whole Laprairie basin as well as along the St. Lawrence river from Montreal down to Sorel. It therefore becomes extremely important for the metropolitan area of Montreal to have adequate transportation facilities.
With that in mind I am sure the house and the minister will not begrudge my saying that when the St. Lawrence seaway was built provision was made for the construction of approaches to the Mercier bridge, the one now under construction. Provision was made for the construction of approaches to meet not one bridge, as was then in existence, but to meet a parallel bridge. While the province did, for a period of years, give the indication that they intended to build a parallel bridge to that of Mercier, nothing was done in that regard. I believe that because of the decision, about which I should like to say a word later on, to build the approaches as they were then built, that is approaches of such a nature as to permit the construction of the parallel bridge. We would not have this bridge now. Because of the approaches which were built on the south side it will not be necessary for the province of Quebec to do these now but only to link the bridge with the approaches which were constructed by the St. Lawrence seaway authority.
Here I should like to bring to the attention of the house the fact that this is a vehicular bridge which is located at the head of the Lachine rapids and was built by a private corporation. It was built by La Corporation du Pont du Lac Saint-Louis, which corporation was authorized by a special Quebec act known as 18 George V, 1928, chapter 110. The provision was made for the construction from Ville La Salle to Caugh-nawaga. At the time the Mercier bridge was constructed it was thought that the seaway channel would be on the north side of the river and provision was made in the legislation for the appropriate works to be constructed by La Corporation du Pont du Lac Saint-Louis, and the federal government gave approval to the construction of this bridge upon certain conditions. I should like to put on the record one or two of those conditions:
1.	The corporation undertakes to instal a movable span in the bridge, if and when, in the opinion of the governor in council, such action is required in the interest of navigation, the cost of installation of such movable span to accommodate deep water navigation on the proposed canal section, as well as the cost of operation and maintenance of this movable span to be borne by the owners of the bridge.
2.	The corporation further undertakes to remove, after the completion of the proposed work, all temporary constructions such as cofferdams, false works, rip raps, pile work, etc., from the bed of the river or the site of the work as the governor

in council may direct, in order that there shall be no obstruction in the way of navigation or of the flow of water or of future works.
I am sure the Minister of Public Works will realize immediately the importance of introducing conditions such as these, having regard to the Navigable Waters Protection Act itself. Then there was clause 3 which said:
3.	Should the works mentioned in clauses 1 and 2 not be carried out within the time specified in the notice of the governor in council, the latter shall have the right to perform the same and recover the cost thereof from the corporation.
4.	The corporation further undertakes to maintain at night on the work during construction the necessary lights at its own expense.
5.	The corporation further undertakes, in constructing, maintaining or operating the said bridge, not to interfere with navigation in any way avoidable in the opinion of the governor in council.
6.	It is further understood that the approval of this application shall not relieve the corporation from any liability for damage which may be caused either directly or indirectly by the said work.
The house may wonder why I put these conditions which were in the legislation on the record. I put them on the record for this purpose, and I think the house should know this. At the time the St. Lawrence seaway was under construction a decision was taken in the early years to move the channel from the north side to the south side. A legal point arose as to whether the liability of the province of Quebec to conform to the clauses which I have just mentioned was related to the south shore in the same manner as it was to the north shore.
I must say that we in the seaway authority took the position that they were liable and the government of the province of Quebec took the position that they were not liable. There were several discussions between the minister of transport at the time, members of the seaway authority and the government of the province of Quebec, through several of its departments, including the premier himself, but it was not possible to reach agreement. If the matter had been referred to the courts or had been delayed further it would not have been possible to complete the St. Lawrence seaway in the time required.
I mention that matter at this time simply so that those who are in office now, including both the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Transport, may keep this matter in mind when there is a reckoning of accounts with the province of Quebec. As the house knows, water lots were expropriated-and properly so-under this bridge now under construction and all along the Laprairie basin to the entrance of the Jacques Cartier bridge and certainly there will be moneys owing by the federal government

to the province of Quebec. It may well be that the government will want to take these matters under consideration.
The Mercier bridge in any event was constructed in due course-I refer to the one which is now in existence-under the supervision of the Quebec commission already referred to and was initially operated as a toll bridge but the tolls were discontinued in 1942. The abolition of tolls referred to a number of bridges in the province of Quebec on which tolls were abolished under the provisions of the Quebec act which was known as 6 George VI, 1944, chapter 44, section 13.
The principal features which were mentioned in the discussions between the various departments of the province of Quebec and the seaway authority namely the department of public works which is responsible for the maintenance and operation of the bridge, the department of roads which is responsible for the highway connections, had to do with the provision by the province of Quebec of a four-lane highway on the south shore and connections from that four-lane highway to the bridge that is now under discussion.
I should like to place on record the principal features involved in the reconstruction of the southern approaches to the Mercier bridge. They were, first, the construction of a temporary diversion from pier 14 of the existing bridge to the south shore; second, the demolition of the southerly approach to the bridge from pier 14; and, finally, the reconstruction of the southerly approach to the bridge by means of a steel and concrete viaduct to provide for four-lane traffic ascending on a grade of approximately 4.5 per cent from pier 14 over the seaway channel with a clearance of 120 feet; and descending partly on a steel and concrete viaduct and partly on a fill to easterly and westerly connections with highway No. 9C in its revised location.
I do not know whether the final cost of this work has been estimated but it was substantial. I want to come back to the question of transportation facilities across the St. Lawrence river. Unquestionably the construction of this bridge is going to be of tremendous assistance. However, I am afraid that this will not be sufficient and that a great deal more will be required by way of bridges between the island of Montreal and the shores of the St. Lawrence.
There was prepared in 1957 a study of conditions of traffic over the bridges which separate Montreal from the south shore. I should like to put some of these figures on the record before I conclude. The traffic counts which were made at that time-that was in 1957-indicated that the annual daily 79951-0-330i
Bridges
average for the Jacques Cartier bridge was about 40,000 cars per day. Peak hour flows of 3,500 cars per hour had been registered almost daily while several peaks of more than
4,000	cars per hour had been counted, particularly during the summer season. As to the practical capacity of one bridge, namely the Jacques Cartier bridge, it will accommodate up to 7,500 cars per hour, especially if in the two lanes that have been added to this bridge-one by the former administration and the other by this administration-the traffic is reversible and they are used to balance the directional pattern of the traffic demand.
The Victoria bridge has had a bracket constructed on the downstream side and there is now provision for two lanes of 17 feet wide, one in each direction. These lanes will accommodate 1,800 cars per hour with no trouble. Several counts have shown a density of more than 2,000 cars per hour in one direction. The annual daily average is a little less than 20,000 cars per day.
The Mercier bridge figures which were taken at that time indicated that that facility was going through a complete change-over, following the completion of the approaches which were constructed by the St. Lawrence authority and to which I have referred. The new approaches on the south side, the traffic study reported, will guarantee capacity equivalent to that of the existing roadway. However, since the construction of a twin structure has been strongly suggested for the near future, the study was taking for granted the availability of the increased capacity of the Mercier bridge. When the two bridges, one operating in one direction and the other operating in the other direction, are in operation as twin structures, the Mercier bridge should be easily able to accommodate 4,500 cars per hour. At present the bridge has an annual daily average of about 15,000 cars and peak hour flows of 1,500 to 1,700 cars per hour. But as the study indicated at the time, that was not nearly sufficient to look after the traffic conditions in Montreal. It is true, of course, that a new bridge is under construction, namely the Champlain bridge, which also will link the island of Montreal with the south shore over Nuns' island. That bridge also will assist tremendously.
Here let me bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport, if I may, the fact that that bridge is not proceeding according to schedule. I do not want to be critical in any way but I want to raise the matter at this stage because I find that when these matters are brought up in the House of Commons the Minister of Transport generally takes cognizance of them and brings these suggestions

Bridges
to the attention of his officers. There is no doubt but that the progress of the work on the Champlain bridge is certainly not going according to schedule. It may well be that the majority of the contracts have been let, but I do think-

subtopic: LA SALLE, QUE.  AUTHORIZATION FOR CON- STRUCTION ACROSS ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to hear the hon. member, I think he is making a very good contrioution to the debate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LA SALLE, QUE.  AUTHORIZATION FOR CON- STRUCTION ACROSS ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext: I thank the Minister of Public Works for his intervention and I would be the last one to quarrel with Your Honour's suggestion that I am not in order. But may I draw your attention to the fact that the Navigable Waters Protection Act provides clearly that no bridge across the St. Lawrence shall be built except by special legislation such as this, and I believe this authorizes a member of parliament to deal with all of the bridges that were constructed by virtue of legislation of this character.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LA SALLE, QUE.  AUTHORIZATION FOR CON- STRUCTION ACROSS ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext: I would not argue with that but I did think the hon. member was straying a little in dealing with the rate of progress of construction. However, the house apparently is quite content to have him proceed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LA SALLE, QUE.  AUTHORIZATION FOR CON- STRUCTION ACROSS ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext:
I am not going to take undue advantage of this kindness on the part of the other side of the house, but none the less I was just concluding my remarks on that matter. I would ask the Minister of Transport to bring this matter to the attention of his officers. I think if he does there should and will be greater progress.
Now I come back to the position of vehicular traffic across the St. Lawrence river. I make another plea here for the construction of a bridge east of the Jacques Cartier bridge. I am not going to labour it unduly because this matter was discussed during the estimates of the minister, but I would say that according to the study which was made in 1957 the construction of this bridge, which is the most westerly of the four, will certainly not look after transportation conditions adequately in so far as conditions east of the Jacques Cartier bridge are concerned.
There is, as I have said, tremendous industrial development here, much of it in steel. There are the equivalent of three large steel industries which have been developed in that area. I think the government should give careful consideration to the representations which have been made by its own members and which have been made by the

Associate Minister of National Delence (Mr. Sevigny) following a statement which I made in the house some time ago when I referred to a report on the St. Lawrence ship channel and the Montreal harbour committee in 1950, which report recommended construction of a bridge east of the Jacques Cartier bridge.
All I want to say on that is this. I think the time has come to give consideration to it now, because I know that in order to prepare plans and specifications and to get the various approvals from the province, the municipality, and so forth, time is necessary and unless it is done now and consideration is given to it at this time I doubt very much whether any progress will be made. Where it should go I am not in a position to say. I think that should be determined by a committee, as many committees are established from time to time by the government concerning railways. In fact there is one royal commission at the present time determining what location the Pine Point railway should follow. It might be advisable for the government to estabush a committee which would determine where the location of this bridge should be.
In the eyes of some people it should be at the foot of Boulevard Pie IX, adjoining it with the south shore. In the eyes of others it should be further east of that. As I say, I am not in a position to state where it should be other than to say that owing to the increasing population in Montreal, and because of this traffic study which indicates that within the next ten years there will be an increase of close to one million in population of the city, consideration must of necessity be given at once to the plans for an additional bridge in that area.
I think we on this side of the house are quite happy about the construction of this bridge. We think it is timely. We support it and we trust and hope that it will be built with the least possible delay.

subtopic: LA SALLE, QUE.  AUTHORIZATION FOR CON- STRUCTION ACROSS ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the quite brief but lucid explanation of the purposes of this measure given us by the minister, and the longer and very interesting speech of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), who has a first-class knowledge of the situation along the St. Lawrence and the traffic requirements as a result of the very high position he held in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway, we in this group have no hesitation whatever in supporting this non-contentious measure which provides for the province of Quebec to build a bridge as a transportation facility across the St. Lawrence river to meet the increasing traffic

requirements occasioned by the developments in that province about which we are pleased to hear.

The officials outlined the route, gave reasons for choosing it and dealt exhaustively with this whole project. I can say in answer to the hon. member for Trinity that I will be very glad to see that he gets a copy of the report of the committee. As I say, it covered about a four and a half hour period-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF TERMINAL FACILITIES AT TORONTO
speechtext: How long?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF TERMINAL FACILITIES AT TORONTO
speechtext: It just shows how thoroughly we go into these matters of importance, and it is right that we should. Regarding the time when this project may be started, I may say that as soon as this bill passes, as I hope it will, the C.N.R. officials will begin the preliminary work. subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF TERMINAL FACILITIES AT TORONTO
speechtext:
It is more in sorrow than in anger that I rise at this point to make a final contribution regarding this matter of the bypass line which runs for most of its length through the constituency of York-Scarbor-ough. For the information of the hon. member for Trinity, the subject of employment did come up at the committee. The question was asked, I believe by myself, and the answer was a rough estimate of 5,000 man-years as a gauge of the direct labour content of the project, to say nothing of the endless thousands of jobs created in secondary industries as a result of the large amount of material required for construction.
The committee during its hearings was left, I will not say unimpressed, but certainly unconvinced about the alternative routes which were suggested by various ratepayers whose districts are to be greatly affected by the proposed route. None of the three alternative routes commended themselves to the committee.
There was one unusual aspect. The timing of the committee was such that an opportunity was not given to me at the time to reply to the allegation of an hon. member who made certain comments. I was hoping he would be in the house tonight to hear my reply. Certainly I would like to put it on record. The suggestion made by the hon. member for York North to the effect that the objections to the proposed route in the Thornhill area were largely centred on a
